papers.title: Bridging microbiology and public health through simulation-based learning
papers.abstract: Within our synchronous, online global health-focused upper-level microbiology course, we find that students struggle to translate learning to real-world applications. For examples, consider the recent measles outbreaks and major events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, which prompt many questions about how basic microbiological information is used by public health professionals. To address these points, we created a simulation-based curriculum that places students in an action role during an infectious disease outbreak. Our stand-alone curriculum walks through a historical measles outbreak that introduces outbreak investigation, community communication, and how these depend on microbiological knowledge. By using breakout groups, students have an opportunity to decide classifications, public messaging, and intervention metrics. We provide students with an outbreak investigation reference worksheet and interweave breakout rooms with didactic vignettes covering background information while revealing actual responses to outbreaks in conjunction with data obtained by responding scientists. Students synthesize material and apply it in real-time – allowing them to exercise critical thinking while bolstering relevance of microbiology and public health to popular media.

papers.title: Reading the Infodemic Against the Epidemic: A Real-Risk Benchmark for Inflated and Downplayed Disease Risk on Reddit Within the 2026 World Cup Window
papers.abstract: During the deadly hantavirus outbreak of May 2026, the loudest online response called it a hoax, while measles, the one rising threat, drew little attention. That inversion is the half of the infodemic we rarely measure: not amplified fear, but the quiet downplaying of a real risk. Detecting it requires what the field lacks: an external benchmark for the true risk. Anchoring one in the epidemiological and mass-gathering literature, with the 2026 FIFA World Cup run-up as a dated window, two coders judged Reddit claims about measles (high), hantavirus (low), and Ebola (near zero) for accuracy and direction (Cohen's kappa 0.72 and 0.68). Of 66 coded claims, 41 were inaccurate, and distortion ran both ways: 24 downplayed risk and 17 inflated it (exact binomial p = 0.35), with downplaying at least as common as inflating. Attention ran opposite to danger, hantavirus drawing the most claims (44 of 66) and measles the fewest (8): the infodemic did not mirror the epidemic. The curated, single-platform sample makes these patterns exploratory, but they suggest that defenses built against panic alone miss its mirror image, the denial of a real threat that prior work links to weaker protection among the most exposed.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the discrepancy between public attention and actual disease risk during the 2026 hantavirus outbreak, highlighting the need to understand how online discourse distorts perceptions of real threats like measles.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed Reddit claims about measles, hantavirus, and Ebola during the 2026 World Cup window, using two coders to assess the accuracy and direction of these claims.
analysis.methods: Two coders evaluated the accuracy and direction of claims about measles, hantavirus, and Ebola on Reddit, using Cohen's kappa to measure intercoder agreement.
analysis.main_results: Of 66 coded claims, 41 were inaccurate, with 24 downplaying risk and 17 inflating it. Attention to measles was significantly lower than to hantavirus, with measles receiving the fewest claims (8 of 66).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that public discourse during the 2026 World Cup window did not align with actual disease risk, with measles receiving less attention than hantavirus despite being a rising threat.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study highlights the importance of monitoring online discourse to better understand and address public perception of disease risks, particularly for measles during large-scale events.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's patterns are exploratory due to the curated, single-platform sample, but they suggest that defenses against panic may overlook the denial of real threats, which could impact public health outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the infodemic surrounding the 2026 hantavirus outbreak and measles threat, analyzing Reddit claims during the World Cup window. It finds that public attention was disproportionately focused on hantavirus, while measles, a rising threat, received minimal discussion. The study highlights the need for external benchmarks to assess real risks and suggests that public discourse may not align with actual disease threats. The findings indicate that the infodemic did not mirror the epidemic, with measles being the least discussed. The study's exploratory nature stems from its single-platform sample, but it raises concerns about the impact of downplaying real risks on public health. The results emphasize the importance of monitoring online discourse to better inform public health strategies.

papers.title: A rapid detection of Nipah virus nucleocapsid antigen in inactivated viral cultures.
papers.abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly lethal zoonotic henipavirus that causes severe respiratory disease and encephalitis and remains a priority pathogen for outbreak preparedness. Timely diagnosis is essential for containment, yet nucleic acid-based testing is often impractical in outbreak-prone, resource-limited settings. Here, we report the development of a rapid antigen test for NiV based on a cellulose nanobead (CNB)-enhanced lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA) targeting the viral nucleocapsid protein (NP). Anti-NiV NP antibodies were isolated from human synthetic phage-display libraries (scFv and Fab) by iterative bio-panning, reformatted as full-length IgGs, and screened using ELISA and immunofluorescence assays. Four lead antibodies were advanced to a sandwich-pairing matrix, which identified an optimized capture-detection configuration (mAb #5 as capture; mAb #2 as detection). Bio-layer interferometry confirmed nanomolar binding affinities for the selected antibodies (K D = 39.50 nM for mAb #5; K D = 26.36 nM for mAb #2). The finalized CNB-LFIA produced results within 15 min and achieved an analytical limit of detection of 1 ng/mL for recombinant NiV NP. The assay observed no cross-reactivity with SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, or influenza A, whereas weak cross-reactivity for measles virus NP was observed only at a high antigen concentration (2 μg/mL). Using γ-irradiated cultured NiV quantified by RT-ddPCR, the LFIA detected viral load down to 4.1 × 10 7 copies/mL (4.1 × 106 copies/reaction) by a portable reader and 8.3 × 10 7 copies/mL (8.3 × 106 copies/reaction) by the naked eye. Collectively, this CNB-LFIA provides rapid, equipment-free NiV detection, supporting its potential utility for point-of-care diagnosis in resource-limited settings.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Nipah virus (NiV) is a priority pathogen causing severe respiratory disease and encephalitis, and rapid diagnosis is critical for outbreak control in resource-limited settings where nucleic acid testing is impractical.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study developed a rapid antigen test for NiV using a cellulose nanobead-enhanced lateral flow immunoassay targeting the viral nucleocapsid protein.
analysis.methods: Anti-NiV nucleocapsid protein antibodies were isolated from human synthetic phage-display libraries, reformatted as IgGs, screened by ELISA and immunofluorescence, and paired in a sandwich configuration for the assay.
analysis.main_results: The optimized CNB-LFIA detected recombinant NiV NP down to 1 ng/mL, showed no cross-reactivity with SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, or influenza A, and detected γ-irradiated cultured NiV at 4.1 × 10^7 copies/mL by reader or 8.3 × 10^7 copies/mL by naked eye.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This CNB-LFIA could enable timely NiV diagnosis in resource-limited settings, supporting outbreak containment and patient management where laboratory infrastructure is limited.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to analytical performance and cultured virus detection; clinical validation, field performance, and cross-reactivity with other henipaviruses remain unassessed, warranting a moderate confidence rating.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports the development of a rapid cellulose nanobead-enhanced lateral flow immunoassay (CNB-LFIA) for detecting Nipah virus (NiV) nucleocapsid antigen in inactivated viral cultures. The assay uses antibodies isolated from human synthetic phage-display libraries, screened and paired to target the viral nucleocapsid protein. It achieves an analytical limit of detection of 1 ng/mL for recombinant NiV NP and detects γ-irradiated cultured NiV at 4.1 × 10^7 copies/mL by reader or 8.3 × 10^7 copies/mL by naked eye. The assay shows no cross-reactivity with SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, or influenza A, with only weak cross-reactivity to measles virus NP at high antigen concentration. The authors propose the CNB-LFIA as a rapid, equipment-free diagnostic tool for point-of-care use in resource-limited settings, though clinical validation and broader cross-reactivity testing are needed.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 尼帕病毒(NiV)是一种优先病原体,可引起严重呼吸系统疾病和脑炎,在资源有限环境中,快速诊断对于疫情防控至关重要,而核酸检测在这些环境中往往不切实际。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究开发了一种针对 NiV 的快速抗原测试,使用针对病毒核衣壳蛋白的纤维素纳米珠增强侧流免疫测定法。
analysis_zh.methods: 从人工合成噬菌体展示文库中分离出抗NiV核衣壳蛋白抗体,将其重组为IgG,并通过ELISA和免疫荧光法进行筛选,随后在夹心配置中进行抗体配对以用于检测。
analysis_zh.main_results: 优化后的CNB-LFIA可检测重组NiV NP至1 ng/mL,对SARS-CoV-2、SARS-CoV、MERS-CoV或流感A病毒无交叉反应,并可检测γ射线灭活的NiV培养物至4.1 × 10^7拷贝/mL(读取器检测)或8.3 × 10^7拷贝/mL(肉眼检测)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将该测定解释为提供快速、无需设备的 NiV 检测,适合在 暴发 多发环境中进行即时护理,强调了其在分子诊断不可用的情况下的潜在用途。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该CNB-LFIA有望在资源有限环境中实现及时的NiV 诊断,支持疫情防控与患者管理,适用于实验室基础设施有限的地区。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 现有证据仅限于分析性能和培养病毒检测;临床验证、现场性能及与其他亨尼帕病毒的交叉反应尚未评估,证据强度为中等。

papers.title: VACCINATION STATUS OF PATIENTS WITH CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE FOLLOWED UP AT A REFERENCE CENTER IN BRAZIL
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Patients with chronic liver disease (CLD) often experience varying degrees of immune dysfunction, making them vulnerable to multiple preventable infectious diseases through appropriate vaccination. Objective: To evaluate vaccination status and vaccine coverage among patients with chronic liver disease (CLD) receiving care at a tertiary referral center. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study was conducted at the Hepatology Outpatient Clinic of Hospital São Paulo, Escola Paulista de Medicina, Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP), São Paulo, Brazil. A convenience sample of adult patients with different etiologies of CLD was prospectively included. Participants underwent a standardized interview, review of vaccination records, and serological testing for hepatitis A and hepatitis B. Results: Among 104 patients (61.5% women, median age 51 years), chronic hepatitis C (63.5%) and hepatitis B (10.6%) were the most common causes of CLD. Advanced liver fibrosis was identified in 46.1% of the patients. Vaccination records were available for 82.7% of participants, but only 45.1% showed serological evidence of hepatitis B immunization (anti-HBs positive). Positive anti-HAV IgG serology was detected in 75% of patients, whereas only 14.4% had documented hepatitis A vaccination. Vaccination coverage for other vaccines was as follows: meningococcal conjugate vaccine (8.7%), pneumococcal vaccine PPSV23 (25%), influenza vaccine (53.8%), tetanus-diphtheria vaccine (60.6%), measles-mumps-rubella vaccine (23%), yellow fever vaccine (28.8%), and COVID-19 vaccination coverage was 92.3%. Conclusion: Vaccination coverage among patients with chronic liver disease remained lower than expected for several recommended vaccines, even in a specialized referral center. These findings highlight the importance of systematic assessment of immunization status and reinforcement of vaccination strategies in patients with chronic liver disease.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the vaccination status of patients with chronic liver disease (CLD) at a reference center in Brazil. The central question is whether these patients are adequately vaccinated against preventable infectious diseases, given their immune dysfunction.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a cross-sectional observational study conducted at the Hepatology Outpatient Clinic of Hospital São Paulo, Escola Paulista de Medicina, Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP), São Paulo, Brazil. It uses a convenience sample of adult patients with different etiologies of CLD. Participants underwent a standardized interview, review of vaccination records, and serological testing for hepatitis A and hepatitis B.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Among 104 patients, chronic hepatitis C was the most common cause of CLD (63.5%), followed by hepatitis B (10.6%). Advanced liver fibrosis was identified in 46.1% of the patients. Only 45.1% showed serological evidence of hepatitis B immunization, and 75% had positive anti-HAV IgG serology, though only 14.4% had documented hepatitis A vaccination. Vaccination coverage for other vaccines was also lower than expected, with only 23% having measles-mumps-rubella vaccine documentation.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights a gap in vaccination coverage for several recommended vaccines among patients with CLD, even in a specialized referral center. The study does not provide information on the reasons for low vaccination rates or the effectiveness of vaccination strategies in this population.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings emphasize the need for systematic assessment of immunization status and reinforcement of vaccination strategies in patients with chronic liver disease. This includes improving documentation and ensuring that patients receive recommended vaccines despite their immune dysfunction.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates the vaccination status of patients with chronic liver disease (CLD) at a tertiary referral center in Brazil. It highlights that despite immune dysfunction, vaccination coverage for several recommended vaccines remains lower than expected. The study identifies chronic hepatitis C as the most common cause of CLD and notes that only 45.1% of patients showed serological evidence of hepatitis B immunization. The review underscores the importance of systematic immunization assessments and improved vaccination strategies for this vulnerable population.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述关注巴西一家参考中心慢性肝病(CLD)患者的疫苗接种状况。核心问题是:考虑到其免疫功能障碍,这些患者是否已充分接种可预防传染病的疫苗?
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本综述为一项横断面观察性研究,在圣保罗大学医学院附属医院圣保罗医院肝病门诊进行。研究采用不同病因慢性肝病成人患者的方便样本。参与者接受标准化访谈、疫苗接种记录查阅及甲型肝炎和乙型肝炎血清学检测。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 在104名患者中,慢性丙型肝炎是最常见的慢性肝病病因(63.5%),其次为乙型肝炎(10.6%)。46.1%的患者存在进展期肝纤维化。仅45.1%显示乙型肝炎免疫血清学证据,75%的患者检测到抗-HAV IgG阳性,但仅14.4%记录有甲型肝炎疫苗接种史。其他疫苗的接种覆盖率亦低于预期,仅23%的患者记录有麻疹-腮腺炎-风疹疫苗接种史。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本综述凸显了慢性肝病患者在多项推荐疫苗接种覆盖率方面存在差距,即便在专科转诊中心亦是如此。研究未提供低疫苗接种率的原因或此类人群疫苗接种策略有效性的信息。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 研究结果强调了系统评估慢性肝病患者免疫状况及加强其疫苗接种策略的必要性。这包括改善接种记录并确保患者在免疫功能障碍情况下仍能接种推荐疫苗。

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述关注巴西一家参考中心慢性肝病(CLD)患者的疫苗接种状况。核心问题是:考虑到其免疫功能障碍,这些患者是否已充分接种可预防传染病的疫苗?
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本综述为一项横断面观察性研究,在圣保罗大学医学院附属医院圣保罗医院肝病门诊进行。研究采用不同病因慢性肝病成人患者的方便样本。参与者接受标准化访谈、疫苗接种记录查阅及甲型肝炎和乙型肝炎血清学检测。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 在104名患者中,慢性丙型肝炎是最常见的慢性肝病病因(63.5%),其次为乙型肝炎(10.6%)。46.1%的患者存在进展期肝纤维化。仅45.1%显示乙型肝炎免疫血清学证据,75%的患者检测到抗-HAV IgG阳性,但仅14.4%记录有甲型肝炎疫苗接种史。其他疫苗的接种覆盖率亦低于预期,仅23%的患者记录有麻疹-腮腺炎-风疹疫苗接种史。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本综述凸显了慢性肝病患者在多项推荐疫苗接种覆盖率方面存在差距,即便在专科转诊中心亦是如此。研究未提供低疫苗接种率的原因或此类人群疫苗接种策略有效性的信息。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 研究结果强调了系统评估慢性肝病患者免疫状况及加强其疫苗接种策略的必要性。这包括改善接种记录并确保患者在免疫功能障碍情况下仍能接种推荐疫苗。

papers.full_text: Pascal Muijtjens My son Max was a 28-year-old medical student when he died of measles in 2025. Four years earlier, he had been treated for acute leukemia, first with chemotherapy, then with a bone marrow donation from his brother. When the cancer returned, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy — a form of immunotherapy that re-engineers a patient’s own immune cells to fight cancer — brought him back once more. At the time, he was doing a bachelor’s degree in health and life sciences, and these experiences shaped his sense of purpose. He decided he wanted to become an oncologist, to help others fight what he had endured. During his hospital admissions, he passed the highly competitive selection process for the four-year medical program in Amsterdam. By his third year of medical school, Max was thriving. I watched him rotate through hospitals with curiosity and enthusiasm, drawing energy from his contact with patients and from exploring the breadth of medical specialties. Seeing him wear his white coat after years of treatment and uncertainty filled me with pride and relief. I deeply admired the way he transformed his own recovery from leukemia into a source of strength for others, using his experience to support patients facing their own health challenges. Max remained on immunosuppressive medication for graft-versus-host-disease and, in preparation for his clinical rotations, he had been counselled extensively on infection prevention and control, including the risks of health care–associated transmission. Determined to resume his life and medical training, he followed these precautions carefully. As his father, I felt the tension between wanting to protect him from every possible risk and encouraging him to reclaim the life he had fought so hard to regain. He had received all recommended catch-up vaccines except for the live-attenuated measles vaccine, which he couldn’t take because he was immunocompromised. We just had to trust he’d be safe. Then one day in May 2025, Max fell ill. It began with fever, cough, and conjunctivitis. When he developed respiratory distress, he became a patient at the teaching hospital where he studied and worked. Although the initial concern was for another post-transplant infection, testing confirmed measles. Max knew what that meant. No antiviral cure existed; the only defense was his immune system, and his had not yet recovered. Together, we had faced leukemia, transplantation, and years of uncertainty. Measles, a preventable disease that many still think of as an innocent childhood illness, was never something I imagined could threaten his life. “This is much worse than cancer,” Max said from his hospital bed, as he became increasingly short of breath. In the days that followed, I saw him struggle with intense pain and overwhelming discomfort. He wanted to keep fighting, but as his condition worsened, so did the pain and his anxiety. Despite intensive care and ECMO support, Max died three weeks later. Autopsy revealed diffuse pneumonia caused by measles. We were devastated. It remains difficult to comprehend how it could have happened. The source of Max’s infection was never identified. Despite a thorough investigation, Dutch public health authorities were unable to determine where or from whom he had acquired the virus. His case occurred against a backdrop of declining measles vaccination coverage in the Netherlands, a pattern shared by many countries in recent years. In the months since my son died, I have shared his story widely in Dutch and Norwegian media. I continue to share his story because I want people to understand what declining immunization rates mean for individuals who cannot receive all vaccines. This is not an abstract debate for me. I lost my son because he depended on the immunity of others, and others let him down. I want physicians who counsel vaccine-hesitant patients to help them understand what their choices can mean for those who cannot protect themselves. Kevin Meesters I did not know Max. I’m a Canadian doctor who was born and raised in the Netherlands. When I read about his story in the news, I felt grief and reached out to Pascal. What stayed with me was not only that Max was a medical trainee, a future colleague, but that his story brought into focus a tension I increasingly encounter in my work: caring for patients with weakened immune systems while also counselling a growing number of families who feel uncertain about vaccination. Max’s death transformed that tension from an abstract public health concern into a real story of a young man whose life depended on the choices of others. I do not want to assign blame for Max’s death. In my practice, I rarely encounter indifference about vaccines; more often, I meet uncertainty shaped by lived experience, mistrust, or conflicting information. Still, individual choice shapes collective risk, and when vaccine coverage declines, the consequences are borne most heavily by the vulnerable. Canada lost its measles elimination status in 2025 after more than a year of increasing transmission. The Netherlands has had sustained transmission as well, and the countries face similar issues maintaining vaccination coverage. Against this backdrop, vaccine conversations have taken on greater urgency. I try to approach them with a trauma-informed, nonjudgmental stance, recognizing that hesitancy often reflects fear, prior negative experiences, or exposure to conflicting information. Since learning of Max’s death, however, I always ask families to consider others, often strangers, who depend on them. I try to understand what lies beneath the hesitation, offer clear evidence, and address practical barriers. Trust builds slowly. Max was well on his way to becoming a physician who might have guided others through the illness he had survived. His tragic and avoidable death represents not only the loss of a son but of a colleague whose lived experience would have shaped his care of many others. I can do nothing to change what happened to a son, a brother, a partner, and a young, promising medical student, but I can honour him by urging patients to protect those whose lives depend on the decisions of strangers. Footnotes This article has been peer reviewed. This is a true story.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study highlights the risk of measles for immunocompromised individuals and the broader public health implications of declining vaccination rates, emphasizing the importance of community immunity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a narrative case report detailing the experience of a 28-year-old medical student who died from measles after receiving a bone marrow transplant for leukemia and being immunocompromised due to graft-versus-host-disease medication.
analysis.methods: The case was documented through personal accounts, medical records, and public health investigations, which included testing to confirm measles as the cause of infection and an autopsy to determine the cause of death.
analysis.main_results: The patient developed respiratory distress and was diagnosed with measles, leading to diffuse pneumonia and ultimately his death three weeks later. Public health authorities could not trace the source of the infection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret Max's death as a tragic example of how declining vaccination rates can endanger individuals who rely on herd immunity, and they highlight the personal and professional impact of such choices.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the critical role of vaccination in protecting immunocompromised individuals and emphasize the need for public health messaging that addresses vaccine hesitancy with empathy and evidence.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a single case and lacks statistical analysis, but it provides a compelling, real-world example of the consequences of low vaccination coverage, supporting a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes the death of a 28-year-old medical student, Max, who succumbed to measles despite being immunocompromised following a bone marrow transplant for leukemia. The study emphasizes the need for public health efforts to maintain high vaccination coverage to safeguard the most vulnerable members of society.

papers.source_body_en: Pascal Muijtjens My son Max was a 28-year-old medical student when he died of measles in 2025. Four years earlier, he had been treated for acute leukemia, first with chemotherapy, then with a bone marrow donation from his brother. When the cancer returned, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy — a form of immunotherapy that re-engineers a patient’s own immune cells to fight cancer — brought him back once more. At the time, he was doing a bachelor’s degree in health and life sciences, and these experiences shaped his sense of purpose. He decided he wanted to become an oncologist, to help others fight what he had endured. During his hospital admissions, he passed the highly competitive selection process for the four-year medical program in Amsterdam. By his third year of medical school, Max was thriving. I watched him rotate through hospitals with curiosity and enthusiasm, drawing energy from his contact with patients and from exploring the breadth of medical specialties. Seeing him wear his white coat after years of treatment and uncertainty filled me with pride and relief. I deeply admired the way he transformed his own recovery from leukemia into a source of strength for others, using his experience to support patients facing their own health challenges. Max remained on immunosuppressive medication for graft-versus-host-disease and, in preparation for his clinical rotations, he had been counselled extensively on infection prevention and control, including the risks of health care–associated transmission. Determined to resume his life and medical training, he followed these precautions carefully. analysis.brief_en: The Maryland Department of Health has declared a measles outbreak in three counties: Talbot, Washington, and Wicomico. This official statement was published on August 24, 2026. The outbreak is confirmed, but no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported in the evidence. The health department is conducting an investigation, but details on testing, isolation, contact tracing, or prevention measures are not included. The outbreak is part of the broader public health response to measles, which is a highly contagious viral disease. The declaration highlights the need for increased vigilance and potential interventions to control the spread of the virus within these communities.

Photograph: BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania Deaths from disease are first in state in 35 years and just one day after Maryland declared outbreak in three counties Two unvaccinated individuals have died of measles in Pennsylvania, state health officials announced on Tuesday. The deaths are the first in the state in 35 years and have been announced just one day after Maryland declared a measles outbreak in three counties. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, and is preventable with a highly effective vaccine. “My deepest sympathies are with the loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss,” said the Pennsylvania secretary of health, Dr Debra Bogen, in a statement. “Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness.” Measles kills one to three people for every 1,000 it infects, and can lead to short- and long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling. About 20% of unvaccinated people who contract measles will be hospitalized. “As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand that the [measles, mumps and rubella] vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles,” said Bogen, referring to what clinicians call the MMR vaccine. On Monday, Maryland declared a measles outbreak in St Mary’s, Carroll and Cecil counties. There are 31 confirmed cases in the state. New York urged residents to get vaccinated on Monday, citing an uptick in cases in rural parts of the state around the capital, central and western regions. “The overall risk remains low if you are fully vaccinated,” said Maryland’s health department secretary, Dr Meena Seshamani, in a statement. “We ask that Marylanders join us in our effort to help keep our youngest safe and protect those who are most at risk. Checking your vaccination status and getting vaccinated if you are not up-to-date is the simplest and most effective way to do that.” The news comes just one week after the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released data showing the largest ever one-year increase in requests for vaccine exemptions – the process by which parents can request not to have their child vaccinated and still send them to school. The same data showed a long, slow decline in vaccination rates, particularly for measles. The news also comes after Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, held a press conference in which they linked vaccines to autism, a decades-old claim from the anti-vaccine movement that has been repeatedly debunked by scientific studies. Pennsylvania state officials said both individuals who died from measles were residents of Lancaster county. No further information was released. The state has counted nearly 400 cases across 28 counties in Pennsylvania, nearly half of which are in southern Lancaster county. Most of the cases reported to state health authorities are in adults between 18 and 49. Official tallies are typically an undercount of actual cases. analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 宾夕法尼亚州官员未发布进一步信息。该州卫生部长Debra Bogen博士强调了疫苗接种的重要性及MMR疫苗的安全性。美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)报告麻疹疫苗豁免申请激增,这可能加剧麻疹传播。

news.content: Skip to main content Search Query Show Search TEXAS NEWS HEALTH & WELLNESS EDUCATION POLITICS ARTS & CULTURE NEWSLETTERS WAKE UP with KERA News KERA News Weekday Update Newsletter Signup WAKE UP with KERA News KERA News Weekday Update Newsletter Signup ABOUT RADIO SCHEDULE KERA STAFF CONTACT CAREERS RADIO SCHEDULE KERA STAFF CONTACT CAREERS © 2026 KERA News Menu NPR for North Texas Show Search Search Query Donate KERA News BBC World Service KERA News BBC World Service Next Up: 12:00 AM BBC World Service 0:00 0:00 BBC World Service KERA News 0:00 0:00 Available On Air Stations On Air Now Playing KERA News All Streams TEXAS NEWS HEALTH & WELLNESS EDUCATION POLITICS ARTS & CULTURE NEWSLETTERS WAKE UP with KERA News KERA News Weekday Update Newsletter Signup WAKE UP with KERA News KERA News Weekday Update Newsletter Signup ABOUT RADIO SCHEDULE KERA STAFF CONTACT CAREERS RADIO SCHEDULE KERA STAFF CONTACT CAREERS Health & Wellness Dallas County health officials confirm measles case, warn other North Texans of possible exposure KERA | By Abigail Ruhman Published August 26, 2026 at 10:54 AM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Shutterstock / Shutterstock Dallas County Health and Human Services said Tuesday an individual who later tested positive for measles visited three North Texas locations on Aug. 14 and Aug. 15. The highly contagious virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves the area. Dallas County health officials are warning of possible measles exposure after a resident tested positive for the virus. Dallas County Health and Human Services said Tuesday the individual visited three North Texas locations while infectious on Aug. 14 and Aug. 15. The highly contagious virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves the area. Dallas County identified the following windows of risk: Turrentine Jackson Morrow Chapel, 2525 Central Expressway North, Allen, 75013 Full window of risk: Friday, Aug. 14 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Gloria’s Restaurant, 152 Fountain Circle, Fairview, 75069 Full window of risk: Friday, Aug. 14 from 12:30 p.m. to 5 p.m. The Revel Patio Grill, 9305 Preston Rd, Frisco, 75033 Full window of risk: Saturday, Aug. 15 from 7:45 p.m. to midnight Advice from health officials “If you were at one of these locations during the identified time period, check your vaccination status and watch closely for symptoms,” Dr. Philip Huang, director of the Dallas County health department, said in a statement. “Most importantly, make sure you and your family are up to date on the MMR vaccine.” Dallas County Health and Human Services said people who are concerned about exposure should check if they’ve gotten the MMR vaccine. The department said people who have documentation of vaccination, “laboratory evidence of immunity” or confirmation of previous measles infection are considered protected against the virus. It also said people born before 1957 are also generally presumed to have immunity. People who are unvaccinated and were present at any of the three locations during a window of potential risk should monitor for symptoms for 21 days after exposure. Symptoms can include high fever, cough, runny nose, a progressive rash that begins on the face and spreads down the body and red, watery eyes. Infants, pregnant people “without evidence of immunity” and people with severely weakened immune systems are at an increased risk for serious complications from a measles infection. County health officials said anyone in higher risk groups who may have been exposed to the virus should contact a healthcare provider for guidance. The health department said people who develop symptoms of measles should stay home and avoid contact with others. It also urges people to call the healthcare provider or emergency department before arriving to tell them about the potential exposure to measles. When traveling to healthcare facilities, the county said people who are showing symptoms should avoid public transportation, taxis and ride-share services. Rising concerns about measles The number of measles cases is higher than it’s been in 35 years, with more than 2,750 cases reported across the country – already surpassing last year’s total of about 2,300, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. North Texas health officials said they’re concerned about declining vaccination rates, especially as students head back to school. They said falling rates could lead to even more outbreaks, like the historic 2025 measles outbreak in West Texas – which lasted for months and resulted in more than 750 cases across 37 counties. “Measles is one of the most contagious diseases we know, but it is also highly preventable,” said Huang. “Vaccination remains our best protection against measles and the best way to prevent further spread in our community.” Abigail Ruhman is KERA’s health reporter. Got a tip? Email Abigail at aruhman@kera.org. KERA News is made possible through the generosity of our members. If you find this reporting valuable, consider making a tax-deductible gift today. Thank you. news.source_body_en: Dallas County health officials confirmed a measles case on August 26, 2026, and issued warnings about possible exposure at three locations in North Texas: Turrentine Jackson Morrow Chapel, Gloria’s Restaurant, and The Revel Patio Grill. The individual was infectious during specific time windows on August 25, 2026. Health officials emphasized the importance of the MMR vaccine, noting that unvaccinated individuals and high-risk groups, such as infants, pregnant people without immunity, and those with weakened immune systems, are at increased risk for serious complications. They advised exposed individuals to check their vaccination status and monitor for symptoms for 21 days. Those showing symptoms should avoid public transportation and inform healthcare providers before visiting. The case is part of a national rise in measles cases, with over 2,750 reported in 2026, raising concerns about declining vaccination rates and potential outbreaks.

Britannica Editors Last updated Aug. 25, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Quick Summary Table of Contents Table of Contents Quick Summary Ask Anything Top Questions What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, a hallmark symptom of which is a blotchy rash. It is most common in children and can be prevented through vaccination. What happens if you get measles? If you get measles, you are likely to develop a high fever, cough, and runny nose and have red, watery eyes. These symptoms are followed by a characteristic rash that spreads from the face downward. Symptoms appear 7–14 days after exposure and can lead to severe complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis (brain inflammation), diarrhea, or death, particularly in people who are unvaccinated. Can you get measles if you had a vaccine? It is possible, though rare, to get measles even after being vaccinated. Such breakthrough infections occur because the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, is about 97 percent effective after two doses. However, vaccinated individuals who become infected usually experience a milder illness and are less likely to spread it to others, providing crucial protection for vulnerable populations, including the very young and the elderly. Why is measles coming back? Measles is resurging primarily due to declining vaccination rates, which have dropped below the 95 percent threshold required for herd immunity. Increased vaccine hesitancy and interruptions in routine immunization schedules, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, have been major contributing factors to this decline. Because the measles virus is highly contagious, it spreads easily and quickly through under-vaccinated communities. What is the recommended treatment for measles? No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. What are complications of measles? Measles complications are frequent and include superimposed bacterial ear infection, pneumonia, and lung infection. The virus can also cause hepatitis, appendicitis, and gangrene of the extremities. Encephalitis is a rare occurrence. Deaths attributed to measles usually result from secondary bronchopneumonia caused by bacterial organisms entering the inflamed bronchial tree. Can measles affect adults? Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. Is there a vaccine for measles? Measles vaccines are live vaccines that work against measles alone or in combination with other agents, specifically with rubella (MR), mumps and rubella (MMR), or mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV). The vaccines are typically given in two doses, the first before 15 months of age and the second dose later; timing of the dosages varies by country or region. Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Infants are immune up to four or five months of age if the mother has had the disease. Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. The disease can be prevented through immunization with the MMR vaccine. Learn more in this list of vaccine-preventable diseases. Transmission and symptoms MeaslesGiant cell in a patient with measles.(more) Measles is so highly communicable that the slightest contact with an active case may infect a susceptible person. After an incubation period of about 10 days, the patient develops fever, redness and watering of the eyes, profuse nasal discharge, and congestion of the mucous membranes of the nose and throat—symptoms often mistaken for those of a severe cold. This period of invasion lasts for 48 to 96 hours. The fever increases with appearance of a blotchy rash, and the temperature may rise as high as 40 °C (about 105 °F) when the rash reaches its maximum. Twenty-four to 36 hours before the rash develops, there appear in the mucous membranes of the mouth typical maculae, called Koplik spots—bluish white specks surrounded by bright red areas about 1/32 inch (0.75 mm) in diameter. After a day or two the rash becomes a deeper red and gradually fades, the temperature drops rapidly, and the catarrhal symptoms disappear. Britannica Quiz A Visit with the Word Doctor: Medical Vocabulary Quiz Treatment and complications No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. Although uncomplicated measles is seldom fatal, infection with the virus has been shown to induce a form of “immune amnesia,” whereby measles virus eliminates as many as half of the antibodies generated against other infectious agents to which an individual was exposed previously. Thus, persons who survive measles infection may become vulnerable once again to a range of other diseases, such as chickenpox and polio. By contrast, individuals vaccinated against measles do not experience a loss of immunity to other infectious agents. Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, a hallmark symptom of which is a blotchy rash. It is most common in children and can be prevented through vaccination. What happens if you get measles? If you get measles, you are likely to develop a high fever, cough, and runny nose and have red, watery eyes. These symptoms are followed by a characteristic rash that spreads from the face downward. Symptoms appear 7–14 days after exposure and can lead to severe complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis (brain inflammation), diarrhea, or death, particularly in people who are unvaccinated. Can you get measles if you had a vaccine? It is possible, though rare, to get measles even after being vaccinated. Such breakthrough infections occur because the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, is about 97 percent effective after two doses. However, vaccinated individuals who become infected usually experience a milder illness and are less likely to spread it to others, providing crucial protection for vulnerable populations, including the very young and the elderly. Why is measles coming back? Measles is resurging primarily due to declining vaccination rates, which have dropped below the 95 percent threshold required for herd immunity. Increased vaccine hesitancy and interruptions in routine immunization schedules, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, have been major contributing factors to this decline. Because the measles virus is highly contagious, it spreads easily and quickly through under-vaccinated communities. What is the recommended treatment for measles? No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. What are complications of measles? Measles complications are frequent and include superimposed bacterial ear infection, pneumonia, and lung infection. The virus can also cause hepatitis, appendicitis, and gangrene of the extremities. Encephalitis is a rare occurrence. Deaths attributed to measles usually result from secondary bronchopneumonia caused by bacterial organisms entering the inflamed bronchial tree. Can measles affect adults? Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. Is there a vaccine for measles? Measles vaccines are live vaccines that work against measles alone or in combination with other agents, specifically with rubella (MR), mumps and rubella (MMR), or mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV). The vaccines are typically given in two doses, the first before 15 months of age and the second dose later; timing of the dosages varies by country or region. The resurgence of measles is attributed to declining vaccination rates, which have fallen below the 95 percent threshold needed for herd immunity. The MMR vaccine is highlighted as the primary prevention method, with an effectiveness rate of about 97 percent after two doses. However, breakthrough infections are possible, and vaccinated individuals who contract measles typically experience milder symptoms. The article does not report on specific outbreaks, cases, or containment efforts, focusing instead on general knowledge and historical context.

analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: Measles is described as a disease that spreads easily in under-vaccinated communities. It can lead to severe complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis, and death, particularly in unvaccinated people. The MMR vaccine is noted to be about 97 percent effective after two doses, but breakthrough infections are possible.
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该文章提供关于麻疹的通用信息、其预防措施及流行病学特征,未报告具体调查、检测或防控措施。信息基于历史与通用知识,而非当前病例数据或具体应对措施。

news.content: Skip to content North American Community Hub Statistics Home US Population News Blog Demographics Disease Data Hospital Data Birth and Fertility Mortality U.S Maps Cities Population States More About Us Editorial Policy Contact Us Home US Population News Blog Demographics Disease Data Hospital Data Birth and Fertility Mortality U.S Maps Cities Population States More About Us Editorial Policy Contact Us Search Discover more Vaccines & Immunizations infections City & Local Guides Pennsylvania Measles Outbreak Surges to 424 Cases as Two Deaths Put Lancaster County at the Center of the Crisis Carter Anderson Published: August 27, 2026 Updated: August 27, 2026 Disease Data, News Discover more Healthy Geographic Reference vaccine Pennsylvania is dealing with one of the fastest growing measles outbreaks in the country, and the latest numbers show that the problem is moving well beyond a small cluster in Lancaster County. By Wednesday evening, the Pennsylvania Department of Health had confirmed 424 measles cases in 2026. 94 of those cases were diagnosed in the previous week alone. New infections have also appeared in counties that had not reported cases earlier in the outbreak, including Westmoreland and Butler counties. The surge comes days after state officials confirmed two measles-associated deaths involving unvaccinated Lancaster County residents. They are the first deaths associated with measles in Pennsylvania in 35 years and the first reported in the United States this year. Table of Contents Toggle One of The Deaths Involved an Infant The Outbreak Is Growing Much Faster than It Was Earlier This Summer There Is a Real Risk of Wider Spread Lancaster County Has a Major Vaccination Gap The Next Few Weeks Will Show Whether Pennsylvania Can Contain It One of The Deaths Involved an Infant Discover more Biological Sciences Vaccine Health Conditions State health officials confirmed on Wednesday that one of the two people who died was an infant. The case has drawn additional scrutiny because records from the Lancaster County Coroner do not describe measles as the immediate cause of death. The coroner reported that the infant died from a lacerated spleen. The child had also tested positive for measles. The Pennsylvania Department of Health continues to classify the case as a measles-associated death. It means measles was linked to the case through laboratory or epidemiological evidence, but it does not necessarily mean the virus was listed as the direct medical cause of death. The state has released little information about the second death because of privacy concerns. Another point is important when discussing the infant. Routine MMR vaccination does not begin at birth, so the child would not have been old enough to receive the first standard dose. The Outbreak Is Growing Much Faster than It Was Earlier This Summer On August 25, the state reported 393 cases across 28 counties. By 6 p.m. on August 26, the total had reached 424. news.excerpt: The deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state's health said, and the first such deaths in the U.S. this year, according to CDC.

news.content_title: Two dead in Pennsylvania measles outbreak, first in US in 2026
news.content: News Sports Things To Do Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Two dead in Pennsylvania measles outbreak, first in US in 2026 Saman Shafiq USA TODAY Updated Aug. 25, 2026, 1:04 p.m. ET At least two people have died of measles in Pennsylvania, the state’s health department said, adding that both were unvaccinated. The measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in a news release Aug. 25, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. “Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said in a statement. “As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand that the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles.” Both patients lived in Lancaster County, the health department said, adding that it would not identify them to protect their and their families' privacy. Authorities have confirmed 393 cases of measles in Pennsylvania in 2026, according to the news release. What is measles, and how do you get it? Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause severe short- and long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Nearly 20% of people who contract measles end up in the hospital. Though measles-related deaths are rare, they are not uncommon, occurring in 1 to 3 patients per 1,000 cases, according to Pennsylvania health authorities. "The best protection against measles is getting fully vaccinated," the state health department said. "The MMR vaccine, administered over two doses, boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97% lifetime protection." The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is usually given in two doses around ages 1 to 5. The CDC also notes that adults and teens should also be up to date on MMR vaccinations. Is the MMR vaccine safe? Medical experts have long said the MMR vaccine is safe and effective. For decades, the vaccine has been administered to millions of children, helping prevent severe and life-threatening complications of measles, mumps and rubella. Serious side effects of the vaccine, including seizures, are rare. The vaccine has been available in its current form since 1971, marking more than 50 years of safe and effective use. It also has been instrumental in curtailing the spread of measles, which, before the vaccine's introduction in 1963, sickened an estimated 3 million to 4 million people in the United States every year and causing 500 deaths and 48,000 hospitalizations. Measles cases reach record high Measles cases in the United States have surpassed last year's total and are at their highest since the disease was eliminated from the country nearly three decades ago, according to CDC data. The majority, 93%, occurred in unvaccinated people, and nearly 69% of cases were in people ages 19 and younger. Cases reached a 30-year high in 2025, with 2,289 confirmed infections across 43 states and the District of Columbia. Nearly 90% of cases were directly linked to 48 known outbreaks, and 93% of infections were contracted by unvaccinated people or those whose vaccination status was unknown. Three people, including two children, died as a result of the outbreaks, the first pediatric measles deaths in a decade. Dr. Mehmet Oz contradicts Trump's claims on vaccine President Donald Trump, meanwhile, signed an executive order Aug. 10 calling for more vaccine “flexibility,” fewer childhood vaccinations and splitting the combined childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots at different times. The order also says all childhood vaccines should be spaced out, with each one administered in a separate doctor's visit "to the maximum extent feasible." Announcing the order, Trump said the MMR vaccine could be “quite lethal.” Experts, however, say the vaccine is safe and effective, and research indicates dividing it into multiple shots has no health benefit. Dr. Mehmet Oz, head of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, contradicted Trump’s statement about the MMR shot in an interview Aug. 23 on CBS’ "Face the Nation," saying it is “not a lethal vaccine.” Contributing: Zac Anderson and Mary Walrath-Holdridge Saman Shafiq is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach her at sshafiq@usatodayco.com and follow her on X and Instagram @saman_shafiq7. Featured Weekly Ad

news.source_body_en: In August 2026, Pennsylvania reported two measles-related deaths, marking the first such cases in the U.S. that year. Both individuals were unvaccinated, and the outbreak, which included 393 confirmed cases, occurred in Lancaster County. The state health department highlighted the severity of measles, noting that it has been largely eliminated for over three decades. They urged vaccination, emphasizing that the MMR vaccine is safe and provides 97% lifetime protection. The CDC reported that measles cases have reached a 30-year high in the U.S., with 93% of infections linked to unvaccinated individuals. The outbreak underscores the risks of vaccine hesitancy and the importance of maintaining immunization rates to prevent severe complications and deaths.

analysis.time: The Georgia Department of Public Health (DPH) confirmed four additional measles cases in the metro Atlanta area on August 28, 2026. The measles case was confirmed on August 20, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The cases were confirmed in the Coastal Health District of Georgia, which serves Glynn County and other counties. The affected population includes an unvaccinated resident of metro Atlanta.
analysis.event: DPH also confirmed a measles case in an unvaccinated resident of metro Atlanta.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Four additional measles cases were confirmed in the metro Atlanta area. The confirmed measles case involved an unvaccinated resident. The DPH emphasized that the MMR vaccine is safe and effective in preventing measles.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Georgia Coastal Health District provided information about the measles cases and the MMR vaccine. The DPH confirmed the cases, but no further details on investigation, testing, or containment measures were reported.

analysis.brief_en: The Georgia Department of Public Health (DPH) confirmed four additional measles cases in the metro Atlanta area on August 28, 2026. This follows the confirmation of a measles case in an unvaccinated resident of metro Atlanta on August 20, 2026. The DPH reiterated that the MMR vaccine is safe and effective in preventing measles. The cases were reported within the Coastal Health District of Georgia, which serves Glynn County and other regions. No further details on investigation, testing, or containment measures were provided. The measles virus, historically known as rubeola, is the focus of this report, with no related entities or hard exclusions mentioned.

news.content_zh: 《健康新闻记者协会》(AHCJ)于2026年8月25日发布的文章《宾夕法尼亚州麻疹死亡事件凸显疫苗报告的必要性》探讨了麻疹死亡事件在宾夕法尼亚州的影响,并强调了准确疫苗报告的重要性。该文章未提供具体的病例或死亡人数,但指出因疫苗犹豫及公共卫生沟通不足导致的麻疹 暴发风险。文章呼吁记者与卫生官员提升透明度与对疫苗接种工作的认知。文章未详述任何具体调查或应对措施,而是聚焦于公共卫生报告实践不当的更广泛影响。该内容属于AHCJ为提升健康新闻报道、确保重大健康问题得到应有关注而开展的更广泛工作的一部分。

Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters View image in fullscreen Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, speaks at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington DC on 8 June 2026. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters Vaccine misinformation spreads as RFK Jr suggests two measles deaths were ‘fabricated’ Anti-vaxxers are spreading conspiracy theories after two recent measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania Anti-vaccine activists are trying to track down the families of two people, including at least one newborn, who died after contracting measles in Pennsylvania, as Governor Josh Shapiro tangles with Robert F Kennedy Jr over his “inaccurate and misleading claims”. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), suggested late on Wednesday that the deaths in the state may have been “fabricated” after a Republican coroner – an elected political office in Lancaster county – claimed one of the measles-associated deaths was unrelated to the virus, although the given cause would be consistent with measles. Brian Hooker at Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization that until recently was led by Kennedy, said in a recent video that the organization is “trying to get boots on the ground” and “do outreach” in Pennsylvania. Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania Read more Kennedy is “an anti-vaccine activist in the role of the most powerful public health person in this country”, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “It’s like the world’s turned upside down.” It would be helpful to know the deceased patients’ ages and more information about their deaths, he added. “By not having that information, it allows fertile ground for the kind of conspiracy theory that RFK Jr puts out there, where he said in some posts that these weren’t measles deaths.” The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a Thursday post on X that it was “working to determine what actually occurred”, including “whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles”. The HHS did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about whether Kennedy recommends the vaccine or whether the newly confirmed CDC director, Erica Schwartz, would make a statement about the outbreak and the need for vaccination. About 424 Pennsylvanians have confirmed measles cases, and 73 have been hospitalized. None of the sickened people are fully vaccinated. The two deaths were in unvaccinated patients in Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, which is home to large Amish and Mennonite communities. While these communities do not have religious objections to vaccines, they eschew many parts of modern life, and thus are relatively disconnected from modern healthcare. Few other details have been released about the patients, fueling a firestorm of misinformation from anti-vaccine activists spreading conspiracy theories about vaccines, which are 97% effective at preventing measles. The anti-vaccine activists are attempting to figure out who died so they can reach the families, as they did in Texas when a six-year-old girl died last year, Hooker said. They filmed a misinformation-filled interview with the Mennonite parents in a rare media appearance after their daughter’s death. Hooker also speculated that the Pennsylvania announcement was a political ploy in advance of the US midterm elections, claiming it was “a strategic move” to “get measles deaths on the tip of everybody’s tongue, to get in the forefront”. The Trump administration has at times attempted to downplay its anti-vaccine moves because they are not popular with voters, according to internal polling. When Shapiro first announced the deaths, he pointed to the inaccurate claims from the highest levels of the US government, saying at a press conference: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation.” Kennedy responded on X with debunked myths about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Shapiro called those claims “inaccurate and misleading” in his own X post. When Kennedy offered to help after the announcement of the two deaths, Shapiro asked him to encourage vaccination and stop spreading misinformation, the governor said in the post. The health secretary responded by repeating vaccine misinformation and saying “it would be better if we went back to ‘natural measles’,” Shapiro wrote. “Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others – and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases,” Shapiro added. In 2021, for instance, Kennedy gave a speech praising Amish parents in Lancaster county for not vaccinating their children. “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A,” he said. There is no cure for measles, only supportive care. A few hours after Shapiro’s response, Kennedy posted to X wondering whether the deaths had been “fabricated” and alleging that Pennsylvania was refusing to share information with the CDC. But Pennsylvania notified the CDC of the deaths early on Tuesday morning, before making the public announcement, Dr Debra Bogen, the state’s secretary of health, said in a statement. “I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County,” she said. The cases were also thoroughly investigated by the state’s epidemiology team, and both individuals tested positive for measles, she added. One of the deaths was in a newborn who tested positive for measles, the department of health said on Facebook. Stephen Diamantoni, the coroner for Lancaster county, told the Philadelphia Inquirer that a test on the baby’s lung tissue after death indicated a measles infection acquired before birth. He believes the baby died shortly after birth because of a lacerated spleen. Spleen issues are a known complication of measles infection. Having an enlarged spleen from measles “was not uncommon actually in the pre-vaccine era”, Offit said. The scientific literature includes doctors’ observations of enlarged spleens, which can lead to rupture. “If you have an enlarged spleen and you’re infected with measles virus, the measles virus caused your enlarged spleen. If you then have a splenic rupture which kills you, you die from measles,” Offit said. Anti-vaccine activists have been successful in driving down vaccination rates, Offit said. The ensuing outbreak “isn’t a good look” for them, he said. Children’s Health Defense appeared to want to downplay its role and put out “the same kind of bad information” after the children died in Texas, Offit said. “It’s very easy to convince those parents – very easy – that this wasn’t their fault, because otherwise, they would have to take on the responsibility or the notion that they could have prevented their child’s death.” Hooker complained on Wednesday that the scant details released about the patients made it difficult to reach them. He also noted that his organization was unable to contact the family of a measles-positive adult who died in New Mexico last year, because the state did not release more public information. “The more information that they release regarding these particular deaths, the more that we would be able to dig in and contact family members, get access to medical records and see exactly what happened,” said Hooker. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters Vaccine misinformation spreads as RFK Jr suggests two measles deaths were ‘fabricated’ Anti-vaxxers are spreading conspiracy theories after two recent measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania Anti-vaccine activists are trying to track down the families of two people, including at least one newborn, who died after contracting measles in Pennsylvania, as Governor Josh Shapiro tangles with Robert F Kennedy Jr over his “inaccurate and misleading claims”. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), suggested late on Wednesday that the deaths in the state may have been “fabricated” after a Republican coroner – an elected political office in Lancaster county – claimed one of the measles-associated deaths was unrelated to the virus, although the given cause would be consistent with measles. Brian Hooker at Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization that until recently was led by Kennedy, said in a recent video that the organization is “trying to get boots on the ground” and “do outreach” in Pennsylvania. Two unvaccinated people die of measles in Pennsylvania Read more Kennedy is “an anti-vaccine activist in the role of the most powerful public health person in this country”, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “It’s like the world’s turned upside down.” It would be helpful to know the deceased patients’ ages and more information about their deaths, he added. “By not having that information, it allows fertile ground for the kind of conspiracy theory that RFK Jr puts out there, where he said in some posts that these weren’t measles deaths.” The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a Thursday post on X that it was “working to determine what actually occurred”, including “whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles”. The HHS did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about whether Kennedy recommends the vaccine or whether the newly confirmed CDC director, Erica Schwartz, would make a statement about the outbreak and the need for vaccination. About 424 Pennsylvanians have confirmed measles cases, and 73 have been hospitalized. None of the sickened people are fully vaccinated. The two deaths were in unvaccinated patients in Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, which is home to large Amish and Mennonite communities. While these communities do not have religious objections to vaccines, they eschew many parts of modern life, and thus are relatively disconnected from modern healthcare. Few other details have been released about the patients, fueling a firestorm of misinformation from anti-vaccine activists spreading conspiracy theories about vaccines, which are 97% effective at preventing measles. The anti-vaccine activists are attempting to figure out who died so they can reach the families, as they did in Texas when a six-year-old girl died last year, Hooker said. They filmed a misinformation-filled interview with the Mennonite parents in a rare media appearance after their daughter’s death. Hooker also speculated that the Pennsylvania announcement was a political ploy in advance of the US midterm elections, claiming it was “a strategic move” to “get measles deaths on the tip of everybody’s tongue, to get in the forefront”. The Trump administration has at times attempted to downplay its anti-vaccine moves because they are not popular with voters, according to internal polling. When Shapiro first announced the deaths, he pointed to the inaccurate claims from the highest levels of the US government, saying at a press conference: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation.” Kennedy responded on X with debunked myths about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. When Kennedy offered to help after the announcement of the two deaths, Shapiro asked him to encourage vaccination and stop spreading misinformation, the governor said in the post. The health secretary responded by repeating vaccine misinformation and saying “it would be better if we went back to ‘natural measles’,” Shapiro wrote. “Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others – and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases,” Shapiro added. In 2021, for instance, Kennedy gave a speech praising Amish parents in Lancaster county for not vaccinating their children. “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A,” he said. There is no cure for measles, only supportive care. The cases were also thoroughly investigated by the state’s epidemiology team, and both individuals tested positive for measles, she added. One of the deaths was in a newborn who tested positive for measles, the department of health said on Facebook. Stephen Diamantoni, the coroner for Lancaster county, told the Philadelphia Inquirer that a test on the baby’s lung tissue after death indicated a measles infection acquired before birth. He believes the baby died shortly after birth because of a lacerated spleen. Spleen issues are a known complication of measles infection. Having an enlarged spleen from measles “was not uncommon actually in the pre-vaccine era”, Offit said. The scientific literature includes doctors’ observations of enlarged spleens, which can lead to rupture. “If you have an enlarged spleen and you’re infected with measles virus, the measles virus caused your enlarged spleen. If you then have a splenic rupture which kills you, you die from measles,” Offit said. Anti-vaccine activists have been successful in driving down vaccination rates, Offit said. The ensuing outbreak “isn’t a good look” for them, he said. Children’s Health Defense appeared to want to downplay its role and put out “the same kind of bad information” after the children died in Texas, Offit said. “It’s very easy to convince those parents – very easy – that this wasn’t their fault, because otherwise, they would have to take on the responsibility or the notion that they could have prevented their child’s death.” Hooker complained on Wednesday that the scant details released about the patients made it difficult to reach them. Photo: Erskine Palmer/CDC/Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Two people in Pennsylvania have died from measles, the state's health department said Tuesday — they are the state's first deaths from the illness in more than three decades. Why it matters: The U.S. is currently experiencing its highest count of measles cases in 35 years. The two deaths are the first reported in the U.S. in 2026. Measles is a highly contagious disease that spreads through coughing or breathing. For years, it was a common childhood illness before a vaccine was developed to protect against it. Anyone who is unprotected from measles is at risk of getting it. Driving the news: The two people who died in Pennsylvania were unvaccinated, the state's health department said. They lived in Lancaster County, the epicenter of the state's outbreak this year, which has seen at least 390 cases, the health department said. Lancaster County has historically had lower vaccination rates compared to the rest of the state. The state's outbreak has caused at least 70 hospitalizations. What they're saying: "Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don't fully understand the potential severity of the illness," Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen wrote in a statement. Measles cases hit 35-year high in U.S. By the numbers: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there have been at least 2,777 measles cases reported in the U.S. this year. The U.S. surpassed last year's total for measles cases in July. Three people died from measles in 2025, a year that saw widespread outbreaks throughout the nation. Measles outbreak and the MMR vaccine, explained Zoom out: The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine protects against measles by supercharging the immune system, providing 97% protection for life. Most of the people infected with measles are unvaccinated, the CDC says. "When measles gets into communities of unvaccinated people in the United States, outbreaks can occur," the CDC says. State of play: President Trump announced an executive order in August to split the childhood MMR vaccine into three shots, delivered at separate medical visits. Health experts warned that breaking up the vaccine shots will make children less safe, decrease interest in vaccination and leave communities more exposed to measles outbreaks. U.S. elimination status under threat The big picture: The rise in measles cases last year challenged the U.S. elimination status for measles for the first time. Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. 26 years ago, largely thanks to the country's vaccination program. Many health experts expect the U.S. to lose its status in 2026, given the swarm of cases this year. What's next: The U.S. measles elimination status is scheduled for review in November. Photo: Erskine Palmer/CDC/Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Two people in Pennsylvania have died from measles, the state's health department said Tuesday — they are the state's first deaths from the illness in more than three decades. Why it matters: The U.S. is currently experiencing its highest count of measles cases in 35 years. The two deaths are the first reported in the U.S. in 2026. Measles is a highly contagious disease that spreads through coughing or breathing. For years, it was a common childhood illness before a vaccine was developed to protect against it. Anyone who is unprotected from measles is at risk of getting it. Driving the news: The two people who died in Pennsylvania were unvaccinated, the state's health department said. They lived in Lancaster County, the epicenter of the state's outbreak this year, which has seen at least 390 cases, the health department said. Lancaster County has historically had lower vaccination rates compared to the rest of the state. The state's outbreak has caused at least 70 hospitalizations. What they're saying: "Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don't fully understand the potential severity of the illness," Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen wrote in a statement. Measles cases hit 35-year high in U.S. By the numbers: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there have been at least 2,777 measles cases reported in the U.S. this year. The U.S. surpassed last year's total for measles cases in July. Three people died from measles in 2025, a year that saw widespread outbreaks throughout the nation. Measles outbreak and the MMR vaccine, explained Zoom out: The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine protects against measles by supercharging the immune system, providing 97% protection for life. Most of the people infected with measles are unvaccinated, the CDC says. "When measles gets into communities of unvaccinated people in the United States, outbreaks can occur," the CDC says. State of play: President Trump announced an executive order in August to split the childhood MMR vaccine into three shots, delivered at separate medical visits. Health experts warned that breaking up the vaccine shots will make children less safe, decrease interest in vaccination and leave communities more exposed to measles outbreaks. U.S. elimination status under threat The big picture: The rise in measles cases last year challenged the U.S. elimination status for measles for the first time. Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. 26 years ago, largely thanks to the country's vaccination program. Many health experts expect the U.S. to lose its status in 2026, given the swarm of cases this year. What's next: The U.S. measles elimination status is scheduled for review in November.
