news.content_title: New measles cases in Ohio slow as Pennsylvania reports two deaths
news.content: News Sports Business Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE New measles cases in Ohio slow as Pennsylvania reports two deaths Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Aug. 28, 2026, 4:49 a.m. ET Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 has grown to 107 cases across 12 counties. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, with two recent deaths reported in Pennsylvania. Health officials attribute the rise in cases to declining vaccination rates and encourage the MMR vaccine for protection. Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues to grow, but has slowed down with only eight new cases reported over the past week. The Ohio Department of Health is reporting 107 cases in 12 counties, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Aug. 20. That's up from 99 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 20; 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13; and 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Nationwide, two people in Pennsylvania died from measles, the first of the year, USA TODAY reports. And measles cases nationwide hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released July 22 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashtabula: 24 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 7 Geauga: 28 Harrison: 10 Holmes: 5 Knox: 4 Meigs: 4 Ottawa: 1 Trumbull: 3 Tuscarawas: 12 Wayne: 6 The case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with 45 cases in 2025, seven in 2024 and one case in 2023. Pennsylvania measles deaths At least two people have died from measles in Pennsylvania, the state's health department announced. Both were unvaccinated. The measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in a news release Aug. 25, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Where are measles cases spreading? While Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, the state dashboard shows two additional cases there. The Wayne County Health Department reports some of its cases are likely associated with a previously identified measles exposure event at Smokey Lane Stables, 686 Smokey Lane Road NW in Sugarcreek, on July 17. One of the Tuscarawas cases is from the same event, that county health department reports. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. In Trumbull County, health officials report that infected individuals were at the Walmart in Liberty on July 29 and Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department in Boardman on Aug. 2, during the time they were able to spread the virus. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Why are measles cases on the rise? Ohio vaccination rates Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, USA TODAY reports. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lower overall vaccination rates, according to experts. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. Share on FacebookShare on Twitter Two Unvaccinated People Die of Measles in Pennsylvania as U.S. Outbreak Surpasses 2025 Total Two unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, have died from measles, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said Tuesday, marking the first measles-associated deaths reported in the United States in 2026. The deaths are also the first measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania in 35 years, according to the state health department. Officials said both victims were unvaccinated and lived in Lancaster County. They did not release additional information about the victims to protect their privacy. The deaths come as the United States experiences its largest measles outbreak in decades. As of Aug. 20, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded 2,777 confirmed measles cases in the United States in 2026, compared with 2,289 for all of 2025. The CDC said 94% of this year’s confirmed cases were associated with outbreaks. Pennsylvania had reported 393 measles cases in 28 counties as of Aug. 25, according to the state Department of Health. Pennsylvania records first measles deaths in 35 years The two deaths represent a significant reversal for Pennsylvania, where measles deaths had not been reported for more than three decades. Both victims were unvaccinated Lancaster County residents, the state health department said. Pennsylvania officials have emphasized that measles can cause severe disease, including pneumonia and inflammation of the brain. The Pennsylvania Department of Health estimates that nearly 20% of people who contract measles are hospitalized. It also says measles-related death occurs in approximately one to three patients per 1,000 cases. Measles is exceptionally contagious. The virus spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes and can remain infectious in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours after the infected person leaves, according to Pennsylvania health officials. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are approximately 97% effective against measles, according to the CDC. One dose is approximately 93% effective. U.S. measles cases have risen sharply The 2,777 confirmed cases reported through Aug. 20 already exceed the 2,289 cases recorded during the entire 2025 calendar year. The CDC reported 285 cases in 2024, 59 in 2023 and 121 in 2022. The contrast with the current outbreak is stark. Measles was declared eliminated from the United States in 2000. In public-health terms, elimination means that continuous transmission of measles had been interrupted in the country. It did not mean that the virus had disappeared globally or that Americans could no longer become infected. The United States continues to record imported cases, particularly among travelers returning from countries where measles is circulating. When the virus reaches communities with insufficient vaccination coverage, sustained outbreaks can develop. Five U.S. measles deaths in 2025 and 2026 The two Pennsylvania deaths follow three confirmed measles deaths in the United States in 2025. The CDC reported that two school-aged children in Texas and one adult in New Mexico died from measles in 2025. All three were unvaccinated. The CDC’s detailed review of the 2025 outbreak found that the two Texas children had no known underlying medical conditions. The New Mexico death involved an unvaccinated adult. CDC officials have noted that deaths from measles had been exceptionally rare in the United States after elimination. From 2001 through 2024, only three measles deaths were reported nationally — two in 2003 and one in 2015. That means the United States has now recorded five measles-associated deaths in 2025 and 2026, compared with three during the previous 24 years combined. U.S. vaccination coverage has fallen below the measles protection threshold The decline in measles vaccination coverage is one of the central public-health concerns behind the current outbreak. CDC data show that the percentage of U.S. kindergarten children who had received the recommended two doses of MMR fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. The CDC estimates that approximately 280,000 kindergarten children were not fully protected against measles during the 2025–2026 school year. The CDC says communities generally need vaccination coverage of at least 95% with two doses to maintain the level of population immunity needed to prevent measles outbreaks. The national average, however, conceals substantial differences among states and individual communities. The gap between U.S. states is wide The latest fully published CDC school-year data previously showed MMR coverage among kindergarteners ranging from 78.5% in Idaho to 98.2% in Connecticut during 2024–2025. Only 10 states and jurisdictions reached coverage above the 95% benchmark that year. State Two-dose MMR coverage among kindergartners, 2024–25 Connecticut 98.2% Idaho 78.5% U.S. overall 92.5% The difference between the two states is nearly 20 percentage points. Connecticut reported the nation’s highest kindergarten MMR coverage at 98.2% in 2024–25, according to state data based on CDC reporting. Idaho’s coverage was only 78.5%. State health data show that Idaho also had a substantially higher overall kindergarten vaccine-exemption rate — 15.4%, compared with 3.6% nationally, in 2024–25. RelatedPosts Pancreatic Cancer Vaccine Shows New Promise as Researchers Seek a Way to Outsmart One of the Deadliest Cancers FDA Approves First Oral Drug Indicated to Treat Dermatomyositis in Adults Dr. Irfan Atcha Explains Why the Best Decisions in Dentistry Often Happen Before Treatment FDA Authorizes First Wearable Device That Continuously Monitors Both Ketone Levels and Blood Sugar These figures demonstrate why national averages can be misleading. A state can have vaccination coverage near the national average while individual counties, schools or communities have substantially lower immunity. Pennsylvania is below the national protection threshold Pennsylvania’s kindergarten MMR coverage is also below the 95% threshold. See also Pancreatic Cancer Vaccine Shows New Promise as Researchers Seek a Way to Outsmart One of the Deadliest Cancers State data for the 2025–2026 school year put Pennsylvania’s two-dose MMR coverage at about 93%, according to reporting based on the latest CDC school-vaccination data. Lancaster County, where the current outbreak is concentrated, has an even lower rate, reported at 87.6%. The difference between Pennsylvania’s statewide rate and Lancaster County’s rate illustrates the importance of local vaccination coverage. The CDC specifically warns that pockets of unvaccinated people can exist even in states with relatively high overall vaccination rates. news.source_body_en: Two unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, have died from measles, marking the first U.S. measles-associated fatalities in 2026 and Pennsylvania’s first such deaths in 35 years, state health officials reported on August 25. The fatalities coincide with a nationwide surge in measles cases, with 2,777 confirmed infections through August 20—already surpassing the 2,289 recorded for all of 2025—94% of which were outbreak-linked. Pennsylvania alone has tallied 393 cases across 28 counties. CDC data show kindergarten MMR vaccination coverage fell to 92.4% in 2025–2026 from 95.2% in 2019–2020, leaving roughly 280,000 children without full protection. Measles can lead to severe complications, including pneumonia and brain inflammation, with hospitalization in about one in five patients and death in 1–3 per 1,000 cases.

Now two residents have died from measles SECTIONS Pennsylvania's MMR vaccination rate fell below 95%. Now two residents have died from measles ET OnlineLast Updated: 25 August, 2026 09:57 AM GMT Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size AbcSmall AbcMedium AbcLarge Save Print Comment Synopsis Pennsylvania is facing its first measles fatalities in thirty-five years due to a rise in cases statewide, primarily affecting unvaccinated individuals in Lancaster County. This alarming outbreak underscores the urgent need for improved vaccination rates across the Commonwealth, as national measles cases in 2026 reach levels not seen since the early 1990s. AP Measles is a highly contagious viral infection that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. Two Pennsylvania residents have died from measles, marking the state's first measles-related deaths in 35 years as cases continue to rise across the Commonwealth. Health officials said Tuesday that both people were unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not release additional information about the victims, citing privacy concerns. The deaths come as Pennsylvania has reported 393 measles cases across 28 counties in 2026, underscoring how quickly the highly contagious virus can spread when it reaches communities with lower vaccination coverage. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like ₹29K rent in Noida: Woman shows her semi-furnished flat with swimming pool, gym and other amenitiesThe Economic Times Undo "Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don't fully understand the potential severity of the illness," Pennsylvania Health Secretary Debra Bogen said. The outbreak is part of a broader resurgence of measles across the United States. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded 2,777 confirmed U.S. cases as of August 20, making 2026 the worst year for measles infections since the major resurgence between 1989 and 1991. Live Events That earlier period saw more than 55,000 infections and 123 deaths. Why the 95% vaccination rate matters The Pennsylvania deaths come as newly released school immunization data show that dozens of schools across northeastern and central Pennsylvania have kindergarten MMR vaccination rates below 95%, with several reporting rates of 80% or lower. The 95% figure is an important benchmark for measles because the virus is exceptionally contagious. Public-health experts estimate that roughly 95% of a population needs immunity to prevent sustained transmission. When vaccination coverage falls below that level, pockets of vulnerable people can allow the virus to spread more easily after an infected person enters a community. That makes school vaccination data particularly important because children are among those most affected by measles outbreaks. What makes measles so dangerous? Measles is a highly contagious viral infection that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The virus can cause complications including pneumonia and brain swelling. According to Pennsylvania health officials, nearly 20% of people who contract measles are hospitalized. Deaths remain uncommon but can occur, with the Pennsylvania Department of Health estimating that roughly one to three people die for every 1,000 measles cases. The MMR vaccine is typically administered in two doses during childhood, around ages 1 and 5. Adults and teenagers who are not fully vaccinated are also advised to ensure they are up to date. Is the MMR vaccine safe? The MMR vaccine has been used in its current form since 1971 and has been administered to millions of people. Serious reactions are rare, while vaccination has played a major role in reducing measles, mumps and rubella in the United States. Before the measles vaccine was introduced in 1963, an estimated 3 million to 4 million Americans contracted measles every year, resulting in about 500 deaths and 48,000 hospitalizations annually. U.S. measles cases have reached a decades-high level The Pennsylvania deaths come after U.S. measles cases surpassed the previous year's total. CDC data show that 93% of reported cases in 2026 occurred among unvaccinated people, while nearly 69% involved children and teenagers ages 19 and younger. The country had already experienced a 30-year high in 2025, when 2,289 confirmed cases were reported across 43 states and Washington, D.C. Nearly 90% of those infections were connected to 48 known outbreaks. Three people, including two children, died during the 2025 outbreaks, marking the first pediatric measles deaths in the United States in a decade. For Pennsylvania, however, the latest deaths carry another distinction: the state had gone 35 years without a reported measles death. Now two residents have died from measles SECTIONS Pennsylvania's MMR vaccination rate fell below 95%. Now two residents have died from measles ET OnlineLast Updated: 25 August, 2026 09:57 AM GMT Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size AbcSmall AbcMedium AbcLarge Save Print Comment Synopsis Pennsylvania is facing its first measles fatalities in thirty-five years due to a rise in cases statewide, primarily affecting unvaccinated individuals in Lancaster County. This alarming outbreak underscores the urgent need for improved vaccination rates across the Commonwealth, as national measles cases in 2026 reach levels not seen since the early 1990s. AP Measles is a highly contagious viral infection that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. Two Pennsylvania residents have died from measles, marking the state's first measles-related deaths in 35 years as cases continue to rise across the Commonwealth. Health officials said Tuesday that both people were unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not release additional information about the victims, citing privacy concerns. The deaths come as Pennsylvania has reported 393 measles cases across 28 counties in 2026, underscoring how quickly the highly contagious virus can spread when it reaches communities with lower vaccination coverage. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like ₹29K rent in Noida: Woman shows her semi-furnished flat with swimming pool, gym and other amenitiesThe Economic Times Undo "Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don't fully understand the potential severity of the illness," Pennsylvania Health Secretary Debra Bogen said. The outbreak is part of a broader resurgence of measles across the United States. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded 2,777 confirmed U.S. cases as of August 20, making 2026 the worst year for measles infections since the major resurgence between 1989 and 1991. Live Events That earlier period saw more than 55,000 infections and 123 deaths. Why the 95% vaccination rate matters The Pennsylvania deaths come as newly released school immunization data show that dozens of schools across northeastern and central Pennsylvania have kindergarten MMR vaccination rates below 95%, with several reporting rates of 80% or lower. The 95% figure is an important benchmark for measles because the virus is exceptionally contagious. Public-health experts estimate that roughly 95% of a population needs immunity to prevent sustained transmission. When vaccination coverage falls below that level, pockets of vulnerable people can allow the virus to spread more easily after an infected person enters a community. That makes school vaccination data particularly important because children are among those most affected by measles outbreaks. What makes measles so dangerous? Measles is a highly contagious viral infection that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The virus can cause complications including pneumonia and brain swelling. According to Pennsylvania health officials, nearly 20% of people who contract measles are hospitalized. Deaths remain uncommon but can occur, with the Pennsylvania Department of Health estimating that roughly one to three people die for every 1,000 measles cases. The MMR vaccine is typically administered in two doses during childhood, around ages 1 and 5. Adults and teenagers who are not fully vaccinated are also advised to ensure they are up to date. Is the MMR vaccine safe? The MMR vaccine has been used in its current form since 1971 and has been administered to millions of people. Serious reactions are rare, while vaccination has played a major role in reducing measles, mumps and rubella in the United States. Before the measles vaccine was introduced in 1963, an estimated 3 million to 4 million Americans contracted measles every year, resulting in about 500 deaths and 48,000 hospitalizations annually. U.S. measles cases have reached a decades-high level The Pennsylvania deaths come after U.S. measles cases surpassed the previous year's total. CDC data show that 93% of reported cases in 2026 occurred among unvaccinated people, while nearly 69% involved children and teenagers ages 19 and younger. The country had already experienced a 30-year high in 2025, when 2,289 confirmed cases were reported across 43 states and Washington, D.C. Nearly 90% of those infections were connected to 48 known outbreaks. Three people, including two children, died during the 2025 outbreaks, marking the first pediatric measles deaths in the United States in a decade. For Pennsylvania, however, the latest deaths carry another distinction: the state had gone 35 years without a reported measles death. analysis.time: Measles cases continue to climb in Pennsylvania outbreak, as other states report new cases Meghan Holohan With the reporting of two measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania, there’s a fear the outbreak is undercounted.
analysis.location_and_population: Pennsylvania, United States; two unvaccinated individuals in Lancaster County.
analysis.event: Two measles-related deaths were reported in Pennsylvania, with one being a newborn. The deaths are linked to a measles outbreak in the region.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Two measles-associated deaths were reported, highlighting the potential severity of the outbreak. The outbreak is feared to be undercounted, indicating possible wider spread.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: CIDRAP and public health authorities are monitoring the outbreak and its implications. The situation is under investigation, and there is a focus on understanding the impact of unvaccinated populations.

analysis.brief_en: In Pennsylvania, two measles-related deaths were reported, including a newborn, marking the first fatalities of the year in the United States. The deaths are associated with a measles outbreak that began earlier this year in Lancaster County, where both individuals were unvaccinated. The outbreak is feared to be undercounted, raising concerns about the broader spread of the virus. CIDRAP and public health authorities are monitoring the situation, emphasizing the need for vaccination to prevent further cases. The report highlights the risks posed by unvaccinated communities and the importance of addressing vaccine hesitancy to control the outbreak.

news.title_zh: 宾夕法尼亚州报告与麻疹相关的2例死亡病例之一为新生儿——CIDRAP
news.source_body_en: In Pennsylvania, two measles-related deaths were reported, including a newborn, marking the first fatalities of the year in the United States. The deaths are associated with a measles outbreak that began earlier this year in Lancaster County, where both individuals were unvaccinated. The outbreak is feared to be undercounted, raising concerns about the broader spread of the virus. CIDRAP and public health authorities are monitoring the situation, emphasizing the need for vaccination to prevent further cases. The report highlights the risks posed by unvaccinated communities and the importance of addressing vaccine hesitancy to control the outbreak.

news.title: Measles Kills Two in Lancaster County: Pennsylvania Records First Deaths in 35 Years - Tech Times
news.rss_summary_html: Measles Kills Two in Lancaster County: Pennsylvania Records First Deaths in 35 Years  Tech Times

news.content_title: Measles Kills Two in Lancaster County: Pennsylvania Records First Deaths in 35 Years
news.content: Dr. Jeffrey Gunzenhauser, Interim Health Officer from the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, briefs the media outside the Department of Public Health in Los Angeles, California on February 4, 2015, with a general update of the measles outbreak in Los Angeles County. FREDERIC J. BROWN/AFP via Getty Images Measles claimed two lives in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, on Tuesday — the first measles-associated deaths in the United States in 2026 and the first in the Commonwealth in 35 years. The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed both victims were unvaccinated residents of a county where the kindergarten measles vaccination rate has fallen nearly eight percentage points in eight years, sinking well below the level required to prevent community spread of one of the most contagious airborne diseases known to medicine. "My deepest sympathies are with the loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss," Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said in a written statement. "Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don't fully understand the potential severity of the illness." The deaths arrived in the middle of Pennsylvania's worst measles outbreak in three decades , with 393 confirmed cases spread across 29 counties and 70 hospitalizations statewide. They also arrived 15 days after President Trump signed an executive order pushing to narrow the recommended childhood vaccine schedule from 17 shots to 11 and to split the combination measles-mumps-rubella vaccine into three separate injections — a change that public health experts, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, called "not only disheartening but dangerous." How Did Lancaster County's Vaccination Rate Fall This Far? Lancaster County's kindergarten MMR vaccination rate stood at 95.5% in 2017 — just above the 95% threshold public health officials call the minimum required to prevent measles from spreading through a community. By the 2025–26 school year, it had fallen to 87.6% , leaving more than one in eight children entering school entirely unprotected from a disease with a basic reproduction number (R0) of 12 to 18 — meaning each infected person can pass it to up to 18 unprotected bystanders in a shared space. That 7.9-percentage-point decline did not happen randomly. Pennsylvania is among 15 states that allow parents to exempt their children from required school vaccinations by citing religious grounds or "a strong moral or ethical conviction similar to a religious belief" under 28 Pa. Code §23.84 . The law requires only a written statement — no physician signature, no documentation of the specific belief, no review by any health authority. School nurses across the state have confirmed that these exemptions are effectively automatic. Joshua Good, who heads Ephrata Mennonite School in Lancaster County — where fewer than half of kindergartners were immunized against measles last year — described a decade-long shift in parental attitudes: "The opposition to vaccination has become entrenched in a significant portion of parents, with concerns ranging from how vaccines are developed to their safety to resentment over the handling of immunizations and public restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic." Good specifically named Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as a contributing factor: "And then you throw in messaging from key health people like RFK Jr." Kennedy spoke to roughly 1,500 people in Lancaster County in 2021, at a time when he was a prominent private-sector anti-vaccine activist, and voiced skepticism about vaccines . Nationally, the picture is equally bleak. During the 2025–26 school year, 4.2% of US kindergartners — approximately 155,000 children — had at least one vaccine exemption, up from 3.6% the prior year, according to CDC data published in August 2026 . Vaccine exemptions rose in 41 states and the District of Columbia. The national MMR kindergarten vaccination rate stands at 92.4%, down from 92.5% the prior year — still below the 95% herd immunity threshold. What the Outbreak Has Done to Patients — and What Comes After Of the 393 Pennsylvanians confirmed with measles so far in 2026, roughly 20% have been hospitalized, and none had been fully vaccinated . Children made up approximately one-third of the state's cases. Dr. Fahmida McGann, an infectious disease specialist at Penn State Health Lancaster Medical Center, told a state press conference in June that hospitalized patients this summer have experienced electrolyte abnormalities, kidney and liver dysfunction, and blood count abnormalities, leaving them "exposed to serious organ failures, secondary infections, as well as bleeding." For survivors, the risk does not end with recovery. Research by Dr. Michael Mina and colleagues, published in the journal Science in 2019, documented a phenomenon researchers call "immune amnesia": measles virus infects and destroys preexisting memory lymphocytes — the cells that carry the immune system's learned response to other diseases — reducing unvaccinated children's antibody repertoire by 11% to 73% . The suppression lasts approximately two to three years, during which survivors are systematically more vulnerable to every infection they had previously been vaccinated against or survived — from chickenpox to bacterial pneumonia to strep throat. The MMR vaccine does not produce this effect; only infection with the actual measles virus does. The practical consequence: the survivors among the 393 Pennsylvanians who contracted measles this year have not simply "recovered." Each is now carrying a depleted immune system for the next two to three years, more vulnerable to all other infectious diseases that immunity had previously defended them against, as researchers at ASM document in detail . How the Federal Policy Landscape Made This Worse The Lancaster County deaths occurred in a federal policy environment that public health officials and physicians say has systematically undermined the vaccination infrastructure that eliminated measles from the United States in 2000. Kennedy has held a formal position encouraging parents to vaccinate against measles since the 2025 Texas outbreak claimed two children's lives, but his earlier advocacy shaped attitudes in communities like Lancaster County long before those statements. In November 2025, he ordered the CDC to rewrite language on its website suggesting vaccines may cause autism — a change Kennedy personally directed that directly contradicts decades of peer-reviewed epidemiology. He disbanded the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the expert panel that translates FDA vaccine approvals into clinical guidance. He fired CDC Director Susan Monarez in August 2025 after she refused to implement his vaccine directives, and four senior agency officials resigned alongside her. As of early 2026, 80% of top CDC positions were vacant — eliminating the leadership needed to coordinate emergency responses. On August 10, President Trump intensified that pressure by signing an executive order calling for the number of universally recommended childhood vaccines to be cut from 17 to 11, and specifically directing the administration to split the half-century-old MMR combination vaccine into three separate injections. There is no scientific evidence that splitting the MMR provides benefit , according to Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. The order also directed the Department of Justice to file lawsuits against states that fail to provide adequate religious or medical vaccine exemptions, and directed the Department of Education to cut grants to those states. The executive order was the Trump administration's second attempt to alter the childhood vaccine schedule — a prior schedule attempt had been blocked by a federal court. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) rejected any change to the state's vaccination guidelines. "President Donald Trump and [Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.] are screwing around with the childhood vaccine schedule — ignoring decades of science, sowing chaos and confusion, and spreading dangerous misinformation that puts kids and families at risk," Shapiro said. Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, called the executive order "not only disheartening but dangerous" at a moment when US measles cases had already reached a 35-year high. By that point, 28 states announced they would no longer follow federal vaccine recommendations. What Pennsylvania's 393 Cases Mean Nationally As of August 20, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed 2,777 measles cases in the United States in 2026 — a 35-year high that already surpasses all of 2025's 2,289 cases, themselves the highest annual total in more than three decades. Pennsylvania ranked third among all states in 2026 case counts, behind Utah and South Carolina. Three people died of measles in 2025 — two children in Texas and an unvaccinated adult in New Mexico — all of whom were unvaccinated and none of whom had known underlying conditions. Pennsylvania's deaths are the first measles fatalities confirmed in the United States in 2026. Their arrival changes the political and public health stakes of the outbreak in two ways: it demonstrates that 2026 is not a "high case count, zero deaths" year in which the national consequences of declining vaccination could be argued to be limited; and it establishes Pennsylvania — a large, politically contested state — as the site of measles mortality that can no longer be attributed solely to geographic isolation or extreme under-vaccination in specific sectarian communities. The Pan American Health Organization is scheduled to conduct a formal review of US measles elimination status at its November 2026 annual meeting, with experts widely expecting it to revoke the status the United States has held since 2000. What Does Pennsylvania's Exemption Law Actually Say? Under 28 Pa. Code §23.84, children in Pennsylvania are not required to be vaccinated if "the parent, guardian or emancipated child objects in writing to the immunization on religious grounds or on the basis of a strong moral or ethical conviction similar to a religious belief." The statute requires only a written objection — no physician consultation, no documentation of the specific religious belief, no county health authority review, and no re-certification period. The exemption covers all required school vaccinations, including MMR. This framework creates two structural vulnerabilities. First, it is effectively equivalent to a personal belief exemption — any strongly worded letter citing moral conviction qualifies, making the barrier to exemption lower than in most states that permit non-medical exemptions at all. Kennedy Jr. as a contributing factor: "And then you throw in messaging from key health people like RFK Jr." Kennedy spoke to roughly 1,500 people in Lancaster County in 2021, at a time when he was a prominent private-sector anti-vaccine activist, and voiced skepticism about vaccines . news.content_zh: 2026年,宾夕法尼亚州在35年来首次报告与麻疹相关的死亡病例,该州兰开斯特县两名未接种疫苗的居民因该疾病死亡。这也是当年美国首次出现此类死亡病例。此次暴发疫情为30年来最严重,全州29个县共报告393例确诊病例,70例住院病例。兰开斯特县幼儿园儿童的疫苗接种接种率从2017年的95.5%降至2025–26年的87.6%,低于群体免疫阈值。康复者的免疫系统可能在长达3年内受损,增加其他感染的风险。此次死亡事件发生在联邦政策调整期间,该政策缩减了儿童疫苗的推荐接种时间表,并将MMR 疫苗分开接种,公共卫生专家认为此举危险。该州法律允许学校疫苗接种的自动豁免,导致暴发疫情。宾夕法尼亚州卫生部门确认了死亡病例,而CDC的领导层和指导工作受政策变化影响,包括解散免疫实践咨询委员会及解雇其主任。

analysis_zh.time: 宾夕法尼亚州的麻疹 暴发 于2026年报告,其中两例死亡发生在周二的兰开斯特县,如N2所述。在八年间观察到疫苗接种率下降,2025–26学年显著降至87.6%(N9)。2026年全国麻疹疫苗接种率为92.4%(N19)。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该事件发生于宾夕法尼亚州兰开斯特县,影响未接种疫苗的居民。该县2025–26学年幼儿园麻疹 疫苗接种率降至87.6%,超过八分之一的儿童未获得保护(N9)。暴发在宾夕法尼亚州393个确诊病例和70例住院病例中跨越29个县传播(N6)。
analysis_zh.event: 宾夕法尼亚州兰开斯特县两名未接种疫苗的居民因麻疹死亡,这是2026年美国首次出现麻疹相关死亡病例,也是该州35年来首次记录此类死亡病例(N2)。宾夕法尼亚州卫生部门确认了这两起死亡病例(N3)。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 暴发疫情在宾夕法尼亚州导致393例确诊病例,其中20%住院,且所有住院患者均未完成全程疫苗接种(N20)。康复者的免疫系统可能在两到三年内受到抑制,增加感染其他疾病的风险(N24)。麻疹病毒的基本再生数(R0)为12至18,表明其传染性极高(N9)。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 公共卫生官员和医生批评联邦政策变化削弱了疫苗接种基础设施(N27)。CDC的作用受到领导层变动和职位空缺的影响(N32)。疫苗接种接种率下降被归因于州法律允许自动豁免(N12)。

news.content: Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Local Weather U.S. & World The Scene Politics Investigations Newsletters Clear 76o Watch 24/7 Create profile / Log in Dashboard Email preferences Sign out Trending 🐶 Clear the Shelters 🏈 Commanders 🌡️ Forecast 🔍 4 More Context 👂 All Ears Find Help 📨 NBC4 Newsletters 📺 Watch 24/7 Our News Standards Expand 4 Your Health Maryland declares measles outbreak in 3 counties The health department identified cases St. Mary’s, Carroll and Cecil counties, bringing Maryland's total cases for the year up to 31. By Jordan Young • Published August 24, 2026 • Updated on August 24, 2026 at 6:22 pm Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER Play 0:00 Play 0:00 / 1:28 Unmute Subtitles EnglishNoneSettings ShareToggle Fullscreen NBC Universal, Inc. The Maryland Department of Health declared a measles outbreak in St. Mary’s, Carroll and Cecil counties. The Maryland Department of Health has declared a measles outbreak in St. Mary’s, Carroll and Cecil counties, health officials said Monday. The health department said it is investigating 14 confirmed cases among unvaccinated Maryland residents and that most of the case contacts occurred within specific households. Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. WATCH HERE "I do want to reinforce right now that there is currently no evidence of widespread community transmission in Maryland or in those counties, and most cases that we've seen have occurred among household contacts," Dr. Meg Sullivan, deputy secretary for MDH, told News4. Measles is considered highly contagious and can be spread through the air when an infected person breathes, sneezes or coughs. It can also cause serious health complications or even death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. So far this year, Maryland has recorded 31 measles cases as of Aug. 24, all among people who are not vaccinated, health officials said. Twenty-seven of those cases were identified since July 15. Health 4 on Tour 4 hours ago Community groups highlight women's health, physical activity in Prince George's Crime and Courts 17 hours ago Lindsay Clancy trial: Psychiatrist weighs in on Clancy's mental health In 2025, Maryland only recorded three measles cases. The uptick comes as the U.S. marks the highest number of cases nationwide in 35 years. Preventing measles Maryland health officials are encouraging residents to get vaccinated for measles, emphasizing if an unvaccinated person is exposed to measles, there is a 90% chance they will be infected. To check if you are protected, you can request your vaccination record through MDH here or with your health provider. You can also find information about vaccine clinics in your area here. Most standard insurance will cover the MMR vaccine, which is used to prevent measles, according to the health department. But those who are uninsured can also access the vaccine through Maryland’s Vaccines for Children Program and the Maryland Vaccine Program. "For those individuals that are up to date with their MMR vaccine, the risk remains low," Sullivan said. "So I do think for parents and for families, what we want them to be aware of the information that we shared today, but also to stress that the most effective way to protect yourself is to be up to date with the MMR vaccine and that it is widely available." People who are at risk and have been exposed should watch out for symptoms for 21 days after the exposure. If symptoms appear, isolate immediately and then call your healthcare provider. If it is necessary to see the healthcare provider in person or go to the emergency room, call ahead of time so they can protect staff and other patients. 1:14 What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease caused by a virus that can lead to severe complications and death. What are the symptoms? Symptoms of measles develop over two stages. The first stage typically begins seven to 14 days after exposure. Here are some common symptoms: Fever over 101 degrees Runny nose Red, watery eyes Cough The second stage starts three to five days after the initial symptoms begin and is marked by a rash on the face, which then spreads to the rest of the body. A person with measles is contagious from four days before this rash appears until four days after it appeared. By Jordan Young • Published August 24, 2026 • Updated on August 24, 2026 at 6:22 pm Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER Play 0:00 Play 0:00 / 1:28 Unmute Subtitles EnglishNoneSettings ShareToggle Fullscreen NBC Universal, Inc. The Maryland Department of Health declared a measles outbreak in St. Mary’s, Carroll and Cecil counties. The Maryland Department of Health has declared a measles outbreak in St. Mary’s, Carroll and Cecil counties, health officials said Monday. The health department said it is investigating 14 confirmed cases among unvaccinated Maryland residents and that most of the case contacts occurred within specific households. Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. WATCH HERE "I do want to reinforce right now that there is currently no evidence of widespread community transmission in Maryland or in those counties, and most cases that we've seen have occurred among household contacts," Dr. Meg Sullivan, deputy secretary for MDH, told News4. Measles is considered highly contagious and can be spread through the air when an infected person breathes, sneezes or coughs. It can also cause serious health complications or even death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. So far this year, Maryland has recorded 31 measles cases as of Aug. 24, all among people who are not vaccinated, health officials said. Twenty-seven of those cases were identified since July 15. Health 4 on Tour 4 hours ago Community groups highlight women's health, physical activity in Prince George's Crime and Courts 17 hours ago Lindsay Clancy trial: Psychiatrist weighs in on Clancy's mental health In 2025, Maryland only recorded three measles cases. The uptick comes as the U.S. marks the highest number of cases nationwide in 35 years. Preventing measles Maryland health officials are encouraging residents to get vaccinated for measles, emphasizing if an unvaccinated person is exposed to measles, there is a 90% chance they will be infected. To check if you are protected, you can request your vaccination record through MDH here or with your health provider. You can also find information about vaccine clinics in your area here. Most standard insurance will cover the MMR vaccine, which is used to prevent measles, according to the health department. But those who are uninsured can also access the vaccine through Maryland’s Vaccines for Children Program and the Maryland Vaccine Program. "For those individuals that are up to date with their MMR vaccine, the risk remains low," Sullivan said. "So I do think for parents and for families, what we want them to be aware of the information that we shared today, but also to stress that the most effective way to protect yourself is to be up to date with the MMR vaccine and that it is widely available." People who are at risk and have been exposed should watch out for symptoms for 21 days after the exposure. If symptoms appear, isolate immediately and then call your healthcare provider. If it is necessary to see the healthcare provider in person or go to the emergency room, call ahead of time so they can protect staff and other patients. 1:14 What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease caused by a virus that can lead to severe complications and death. What are the symptoms? Symptoms of measles develop over two stages. The first stage typically begins seven to 14 days after exposure. Here are some common symptoms: Fever over 101 degrees Runny nose Red, watery eyes Cough The second stage starts three to five days after the initial symptoms begin and is marked by a rash on the face, which then spreads to the rest of the body. A person with measles is contagious from four days before this rash appears until four days after it appeared. news.content_title: Health officials recommend measles vaccine after Missouri's herd immunity drops
news.content: MISSOURI—The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services (MO-DHSS) says more of Missouri needs to receive vaccinations for measles, saying that the state is susceptible to an outbreak risk. “We’re below the 95% needed for herd immunity, which means outbreaks can spread fast in our communities,” said the department. “One measles case can infect nine out of 10 unvaccinated people, and the virus can hang in the air for up to two hours after someone coughs or sneezes.” Missouri already has five measles cases this year, according to the CDC . Last year, it had six. “Two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine give 97% lifetime protection," officials said, adding that it’s never too late to vaccinate. Illinois has seen its measles cases drop over the last three years from 67 in 2024 to 14 last year and 4 so far this year. According to Illinois Department of Public Health , nearly 97% of its population was vaccinated for measles as of May this year. Though commonly seen as an irritating rash, the health department notes the virus may cause pneumonia, brain swelling and even death

By: Web Staff Posted 3:27 PM, Aug 27, 2026 LEXINGTON, Ky. (LEX News) — Kentucky's measles outbreak continues to expand, with state health officials reporting 29 confirmed cases statewide in 2026, the highest annual total the Commonwealth has seen since 1991. According to the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services' measles dashboard, 10 new cases have been added since last week. Seventeen of the state's confirmed cases have been identified in August alone. The latest case counts by county are: Christian County: 14 cases Washington County: 5 cases Jessamine County: 4 cases Trigg County: 3 cases Caldwell County: 1 case Owen County: 1 case Todd County: 1 case 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE State health officials say all reported measles cases this year have involved people who were either unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown. No deaths have been reported. An outbreak is defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as three or more related cases. Kentucky officials have warned that additional cases could be identified as investigations continue. Measles is a highly contagious respiratory illness that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Symptoms can include fever, cough, runny nose, red or watery eyes and a rash that typically begins on the face before spreading to the rest of the body. Health officials continue to encourage Kentuckians to review their vaccination status and talk with their healthcare provider about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. The CDC recommends children receive two doses of the vaccine, which provides about 97% protection against measles. The Kentucky Department for Public Health updates its measles dashboard regularly as new cases are confirmed. news.content: Menu Choose edition SingaporeInternational Search singapore asia world opinion life business sport Visual Podcasts STClassifieds Paid press releases Advertise with us FAQs Contact us Pennsylvania reports first US measles deaths in 2026 as outbreak grows Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox The US’ worst measles outbreak in 35 years comes as vaccine hesitancy grows. PHOTO: AFP Published Aug 26, 2026, 08:30 AM Updated Aug 26, 2026, 03:18 PM Set as preferred source Listen WASHINGTON – Two Pennsylvania residents died after contracting measles, US health officials said on Aug 26, the first such deaths in 2026 in the United States, which is contending with the highest number of cases of the highly infectious disease in more than three decades as vaccination rates drop. Both people were unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, which did not release additional details, citing privacy concerns. The deaths come about two weeks after US President Donald Trump unveiled an executive order that criticised the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, calling for the long-used combination shot, which provides 97 per cent protection against measles, to be split up into three separate shots. Trump, contrary to all scientific evidence and decades of safe and effective use, said of the MMR vaccine, that there is a “possibility they are quite lethal” together. The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and CDC offered condolences to the families and said the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), which HHS oversees, was working closely with state and local health departments. “The MMR vaccine provides the most effective protection against measles and helps prevent its spread,” HHS spokeswoman Emily Hilliard said in a statement. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has for decades argued that the MMR shot and other vaccines are linked to an increased risk of autism, a theory that scientists say has been thoroughly refuted by studies examining millions of children over many years. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said he declined an offer from Kennedy on Aug 26 to provide federal assistance for the state’s measles outbreak response. “I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities,” Shapiro said during a news conference. Kennedy, a long-time anti-vaccine activist before taking his post in the Trump administration, is now overseeing a series of studies at his Health and Human Services department examining vaccine safety, including whether they are linked to autism. Trump and Kennedy’s statements and policies have sown confusion and distrust of vaccines, experts said, and have helped lead to the resurgence of a preventable disease that the US had eradicated more than 20 years ago. Public health reversal Two unvaccinated children died from measles in 2025 in Texas, the first US measles deaths in more than a decade and a stark reversal of one of the country’s major public-health achievements. “To hear about the absolute tragedy of people dying from a vaccine-preventable disease again is wrong,” said Angela Dunn, former Utah state epidemiologist and previously a CDC division director in infectious disease response. “We already know how to stop the spread of measles, and it is through making sure that the communities that are most vulnerable understand that the vaccine is safe,” Dunn said. Pennsylvania has been one of the hardest hit states in 2026, with 393 measles cases across 28 counties so far. Lancaster County, in the south-eastern part of the state, has had 185 cases, but these were the first measles deaths recorded in the state in 35 years. The United States has had 2,777 confirmed cases so far in 2026 of a disease that had been largely eradicated in the country, a reflection of declining vaccination rates and policies under Kennedy, who has for decades spread misinformation about vaccine safety. Kennedy in January unveiled a slimmed-down federal childhood vaccine schedule that cut the number of recommended inoculations from 17 to 11, but still included the MMR shot. Those changes were blocked by a federal judge in March. Trump’s August executive order called for similar changes, but the administration is still bound by the federal ruling. “One might think that by now, after more than a year and a half of ongoing measles transmission and outbreaks in the United States, we would be seeing more messaging and support from the federal government,” said William Moss, an epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “Unfortunately, we’re not.” Falling vaccination rates Vaccination rates of 95 per cent or higher can prevent outbreaks by creating what is known as herd immunity that protects people unable to be vaccinated. Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella shot provide 97 per cent protection against the virus. Children typically first receive the vaccine when they are 12 to 15 months old and again at four to six years old. According to Pennsylvania Department of Health data for the 2025-2026 school year, 93.2 per cent of Pennsylvania kindergarten-age children had received the required two doses of MMR vaccine, down from 93.7 per cent during the 2024-2025 school year. In Lancaster County, 87.6 per cent of kindergarten students received the required two MMR doses during the 2025-2026 school year. The federal government and state health officials need to try to identify communities that have low measles vaccination coverage, said Moss. “Many people in this country and in certain communities have a mistrust of measles vaccine partly fed by misinformation and disinformation.” The number of US measles cases in 2026 is the highest in a single year since the major resurgence between 1989 and 1991, when 55,000 infections and 123 deaths were recorded. South Carolina earlier in 2026 experienced the nation’s largest measles outbreak with nearly 1,000 infections over six months. It was declared over in April. analysis.brief_en: In August 2026, Pennsylvania reported the first measles deaths in the United States that year, as the country faces its worst outbreak in over three decades. Two unvaccinated residents in Lancaster County died from the disease, highlighting the impact of declining vaccination rates and anti-vaccine rhetoric. The outbreak has been linked to policies under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, who has promoted vaccine misinformation. The US has recorded 2,777 confirmed measles cases in 2026, the highest in a single year since 1991. Pennsylvania has seen 393 cases across 28 counties, with Lancaster County accounting for 185. Despite the CDC and HHS working with state health departments, the federal government has not provided strong messaging or support, exacerbating vaccine hesitancy. Vaccination rates for kindergarten-age children in Pennsylvania dropped slightly to 93.2% in 2025-2026, down from 93.7% the previous year. Kennedy’s policies, including a reduced childhood vaccine schedule, have been blocked by a federal judge, but the administration remains bound by this ruling. The outbreak underscores the risks of vaccine misinformation and the importance of maintaining public trust in immunization programs.

It delivers clear answers and real-time content based on what people are reading now — showcasing various stories from the WJAC Network that highlight not just what happened, but why it matters. Explore DeeperDive Ask WJAC anything How many measles cases are in Centre County? How many pop-up clinics are scheduled for vaccines? Why are health officials promoting MMR vaccinations? topics: Measles Vaccination MMR Pennsylvania Centre County Pop-up clinics Back-to-school Pharmacies CENTRE COUNTY, Pa (WJAC) — As Measles cases continue to rise statewide, we spoke with health officials in Centre County about what measures healthcare professionals are taking and what they expect to see in the coming weeks. It’s a time that notoriously leads to the spreading of germs as back-to-school season has begun for K-12 and college students. As of Wednesday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health has confirmed two deaths and 423 measles cases across the Commonwealth, including fourteen of those cases in Centre County. The DOH notes that none of these cases have been fully vaccinated individuals. We spoke with Dr. Daniel McKinley of Mount Nittany Health who was able to provide some more information about vaccination options for the public. Powered By 10 Health officials continue to advocate for vaccinations as measles cases rise statewide Share Next Stay He reiterates the message that the best thing you can do to protect yourself and others from measles is to get vaccinated. He says that the vast majority of those who received two doses of the MMR vaccine are protected and do not need a booster. Because of school vaccination requirements, the majority of students in our area have been vaccinated against measles, and because of this, Dr. McKinley says he’s hopeful that back-to-school season will not worsen the spread. He also says that Mount Nittany Health is more than happy to help individuals explore their vaccination options regardless of their beliefs or current vaccination status. “We deal with a whole range of different beliefs and wishes of patients, and our goal is to work with people on what works best for them. And for someone to come in and say I’ve never been vaccinated, that’s not something we’d hold against them in any way, and we’ll be able to talk what their options are, what the risks and benefits are. But I would go ahead and say that the risks of the vaccine are incredibly low.” Mount Nittany and the Department of Health both say that pop up clinics have been assisting in getting people in affected communities vaccinated since late April, and dozens of additional clinics are scheduled for the upcoming weeks. supplementary_news.content: Health First US measles deaths of 2026 reported. How many cases are in Washington state? By Karlee Van De Venter Don Sweeney , 2 days ago A 3D model shows a visualization of the measles virus. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/TNS As measles cases increase across the nation, two people have died due to the “highly contagious” disease in Pennsylvania. The two Pennsylvania cases are the first U.S. deaths from measles so far in 2026, health officials said, and the first measles-related fatalities in that state in 35 years. “People are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illnes s,” Dr. Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania’s ecretary of health, said in a Tuesday, Aug. 25, news release. Neither of the two people who died were vaccinated against the disease, normally considered a childhood illness. This year, Washington state has already reported four times the number of measles cases it logged in 2025. Why are measles cases on the rise in Washington state? Is there an outbreak? Here’s what you should know: What is measles? Where are outbreaks in the U.S.? Measles is a “highly contagious” virus that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The disease can cause “serious health complications,” especially in children younger than 5 years old, the federal public health agency said. Complications due to measles can include pneumonia, “brain swelling, even blindness and death,” said Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease specialist and professor of medicine at University of California, San Francisco. Measles was considered eliminated in the United States in 2000, the CDC said, meaning that the continuous spread of the disease was stopped for longer than 12 months. What counts as a measles outbreak? The CDC maintains a map tracking measles cases and outbreaks across the country. As of Aug. 20, more than 2,700 confirmed measles cases had been reported by a total of 47 jurisdictions, the CDC said. Two states have reported more than 500 measles cases: Utah and South Carolina. However, a state can have a measles outbreak with far less than 500 cases. According to the CDC, an outbreak is defined as “three or more related cases.” There must be a tie between the cases to be considered an outbreak. “Most outbreaks in the United States are small, comprised of six people or fewer, usually within a household,” the federal health agency said. “When measles gets into a community that has lower vaccination rates it can spread quickly, causing larger outbreaks.” The CDC notes that individual states have the most updated information on outbreaks. How many measles cases does Washington state have? As of Tuesday, there have been 55 confirmed cases of measles in Washington state so far in 2026, according to the state Department of Health. Only four of those 55 cases required hospitalization. No deaths related to Washington measles cases have been reported. Those 50-plus measles cases were spread across eight of Washington’s 39 counties. A third of the cases were reported in Clark County, with 18 total cases. In 2025, only 12 measles cases were reported across Washington state. Why are measles cases increasing in the US? About 90% of unvaccinated people who come in contact with measles get sick with the disease , the California Department of Public Health said. The highly contagious virus can live airborne in a room for up to two hours, the agency said, and it only requires a small amount of particles to infect someone. Measles rates are primarily rising due to high rates of the disease in other parts of the world paired with falling vaccination rates in the United States . Of the 55 cases of measles Washington state has seen in 2026, 89% occurred in individuals confirmed to be unvaccinated. Only one case involved an individual who had two or fewer doses of a measles-containing vaccine, according to the state Department of Health. Five measles cases reported in Washington state in 2026 involved people whose vaccination status is unknown. In other words, none of the cases have involved individuals fully vaccinated against measles. Cuts to public health funding have contributed to measles’ spread, Chin-Hong said, along with a wave of fake conspiracy theories that mislead people about the importance of getting vaccinated. What are common measles symptoms? Measles cases typically start with a high fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes, according to the CDC. After a few days of symptoms, tiny white spots pop up inside the mouth, the public health agency said, followed by a rash of small red spots that appear on the face and then the rest of the body. Symptoms typically appear about seven to 14 days after being exposed to the virus, the national public health agency said. Here are some of the most common measles symptoms , according to the CDC: High fever Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Rash Complications from measles usually include ear infections and diarrhea, while more serious complications include pneumonia and encephalitis. “Some people think of measles as just a little rash and fever that clears up in a few days,” the CDC warned. “But measles can cause serious health complications.” Who is most at risk of measles? “Anyone who is not protected against measles is at risk” of getting sick, according to the CDC. According to the Washington State Department of Health, people at higher risk of measles complications include infants under 12 months old and young children who have not been vaccinated. Unvaccinated pregnant people, their unborn babies and people with weakened immune systems are also more vulnerable, the state health agency said. Due to the highly contagious nature of measles, it is important to limit contact with others, especially those who may not be protected via vaccination, if you develop symptoms. “ Measles spreads easily , and people can pass it on before they realize they’re sick,” said Michele Roberts, the Washington State Department of Health’s assistant secretary for prevention and community health. “We all have busy lives, but if you have symptoms, take a moment to pause — stay home and contact your healthcare provider.” “That simple step can help prevent spreading measles to others,” she added. The state Department of Health recommends calling your doctor or healthcare provider to determine your next steps after identifying symptoms. If you go to a hospital or clinic, it is imperative you call ahead to disclose you want to be checked in for measles. What’s the best way to protect against the virus? “The best way to protect against measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine ,” the CDC said. The federal health agency said the two-dose vaccine is safe and about 97% effective at preventing measles. Children can be vaccinated against measles as early as 6 months. The CDC recommends that children get one dose between 12 to 15 months, and the second dose at 4 to 6 years old. Afterthought NFC B-EAST DZTV Just Wondering with Norm The Mom Game Here's To You Here & Now About Us Contact Us Anchors and Reporters Station History FAQ How to Stream Work for Us TV Listings FCC Public File FCC Applications FOX 4 PLUS Contests Brand Spotlight Site Map Regional News Houston News - FOX 26 Houston Austin News - FOX 7 Austin Stream on FOX One Watch NFL Games Watch College Football Games Watch MLB Games Watch NASCAR Cup Series Watch IndyCar Series Watch Men's College Basketball Watch Women's College Basketball Watch WNBA Games Watch MLS Games Dallas County confirms measles case with 3 locations for exposure By Tracy DeLatte and Alex Boyer FOX 4 Dallas County Published August 26, 2026 1:39 PM CDT Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published August 26, 2026 1:39 PM CDT Dallas County reports first measles case of 2026 0:00 2:52 ▶ Dallas County reports first measles case of 2026 The Dallas County Health Department is alerting the public to a confirmed case of measles, with three spots where the patient may have exposed more people. FOX 4's Alex Boyer has more. The Brief Dallas County confirmed a measles case in a resident, marking a potential exposure risk in the area. The patient visited locations in Allen, Fairview, and Frisco on Aug. 14 and 15 while infectious. Officials advise unvaccinated or high-risk individuals who were at those sites to monitor for symptoms. DALLAS - Dallas County is reporting a confirmed case of the measles and shared three locations where that patient may have exposed others. Dallas County Measles The measles virus, paramyxoviridae from the Morbillivirus family, transmission microscopy view. (Photo by: BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) What we know: The patient is a Dallas County resident, but no details about his or her identity were shared for privacy reasons. According to the health department, there are three locations where the patient visited last week, possibly exposing others. Turrentine Jackson Morrow Chapel in Allen from 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on Aug. 14 Gloria’s Restaurant in Fairview from 12:30 p.m. to 5 p.m. on Aug. 14 The Revel Patio Grill in Frisco from around 8 p.m. until midnight on Aug. 15 What they're saying: "Measles is one of the most contagious diseases we know, but it is also highly preventable," said Dr. Philip Huang, the Dallas County health director. "If you were at one of these locations during the identified time period, check your vaccination status and watch closely for symptoms. Most importantly, make sure you and your family are up to date on the MMR vaccine. Vaccination remains our best protection against measles and the best way to prevent further spread in our community." Measles Symptoms Big picture view: Measles is a highly contagious viral illness that spreads through respiratory droplets from an infected person’s cough or sneeze. Symptoms typically start with a high fever, a cough, runny nose, red or watery eyes and white spots inside the mouth. A rash typically develops three to five days after the first symptoms begin. What you can do: Health officials said healthy individuals who are fully vaccinated have a very low risk of contracting the disease. Those who are unvaccinated, too young to be vaccinated or have weakened immune systems should keep an eye out for symptoms and reach out to a healthcare provider with concerns. The Source: The information in this story comes from the Dallas County health department and statements from Health Director Philip Huang. supplementary_news.content: 24/7 LivePhiladelphiaPennsylvaniaNew JerseyDelaware 75° Measles Shapiro, Kennedy have war of words following 2 measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania ByBrenda Goodman, Meg Tirrell, CNN Friday, August 28, 2026 1:46PM There's a public health dispute brewing between Pennsylvania and the CDC, concerning the measles outbreak The Pennsylvania Department of Health this week recorded its first two measles-associated deaths in 35 years, both in people who were unvaccinated. The agency declined to provide further details, saying it was protecting patient privacy. What came next was a war of words. Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, said at a news conference Tuesday that he had spoken to US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and "made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania." Before becoming HHS secretary under President Trump, Kennedy was a leading voice casting doubt on the safety of vaccination. In 2021, Kennedy - then head of the anti-vaccine organization Children's Health Defense - visited Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, where he made light of his own childhood case of measles and suggested that vaccines were causing autism and autoimmune diseases. On social media Wednesday, Kennedy accused Shapiro of fearmongering and the "weaponization of infectious disease" for political gain. He suggested that the deaths there may have been "altogether fabricated" by one of Shapiro's "hopeful staffers" to support a narrative that measles infection is more dangerous than it actually is. He also said the coroner in Lancaster County, where the two people lived, had no record of any measles-related deaths. Pennsylvania's secretary of health, Dr. Debra Bogen, later weighed in, saying she had thoroughly reviewed the case investigation and "sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County, which were reported to the CDC's measles response team early Tuesday morning." On Thursday afternoon, however, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in a statement posted to social media that it was working to determine what had actually happened. "These discrepancies raise important questions, particularly because the Governor's Office has not provided CDC with information relevant to the outbreak and has declined our offers of assistance," it said. The Pennsylvania Department of Health fired back. "It is inaccurate to suggest that Pennsylvania has not provided the CDC with information relevant to the outbreak or declined to work with the CDC," it said in a post on social media. The department said it was in touch with the CDC's program staff and regularly shared data with the CDC. Here's what we know about the cases and the conflict. What does 'measles-associated' mean? Deaths are classified as "measles-associated" when lab testing or epidemiological evidence of measles is present but the disease may not be assessed by the medical certifier or coroner to be the immediate cause of death, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Bogen said she had thoroughly investigated and verified that both people who died had tested positive for measles. The information was not reported until the results of epidemiological investigations were confirmed, she said. Epidemiologic investigations look at when and where a person got sick and how they may have been exposed to a pathogen. Did measles contribute to the deaths? That's unclear. Lancaster County Coroner Dr. Stephen Diamantoni told reporters Wednesday that his office was reviewing the death of an infant who tested positive for measles. He said the child died shortly after birth from a laceration of the spleen, and measles antibodies were present in postmortem testing. Despite the positive measles test, the forensic pathologist who conducted the autopsy "did not feel it was related to the measles," Diamantoni told the Philadelphia Inquirer. Diamantoni said he has no other cases involving people who tested positive for measles. Kennedy and others have seized on that statement to suggest that if Diamantoni isn't investigating, the other case may not exist at all. The state Department of Health countered that "not all deaths are referred to a coroner under Pennsylvania law." Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease physician in New York City and author of the 2025 book "Booster Shots: The Urgent Lessons of Measles and the Uncertain Future of Children's Health," said it's premature to assume measles didn't play a role in these deaths. "The problem is that the facts of the cases are not widely known, which is reasonable, because I think that the Pennsylvania public health authorities want to be careful about potentially identifying people," he told CNN. "Calling something a measles-associated death does not mean that the death was not caused by measles. It means that it is entirely possible that that death was caused by measles, and I would say likely," he added. "And the fact of the matter is that we don't see measles-associated deaths when there is not measles circulating in the United States, and there is measles circulating at levels that it has not in decades, as a result of declining confidence of vaccines, largely from the messaging from HHS and elsewhere in the government." How do these cases fit into what's known about measles? Although details on these particular deaths are still sparse, a growing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania fits a predictable pattern. Of the 424 cases reported in Pennsylvania this year - all of them in people who were not fully vaccinated - 73, or about 1 in 6, have involved hospitalization, according to data from the state's Department of Health. Typically during outbreaks, about 1 in 5 unvaccinated people who get sick will be hospitalized, according to the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases. About 1 in 20 children who get measles will get pneumonia, and 1 in 1,000 will develop brain swelling, or encephalitis, which can lead to brain damage. Even with the best care, measles is deadly in about 1 to 3 people out of every 1,000 cases. The two measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania are the first reported this year in the US, where 2,777 cases have been confirmed. The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine confers a high degree of protection. The recommended two doses are about 97% effective at preventing measles, according to the CDC. That's why experts consider deaths from measles to be preventable. The deaths are "tragic," Ratner said. But so too is the effort to try to cast doubt on them, Ratner added. "It's a common anti-vaccine talking point, and it dehumanizes the people who have suffered and died." "We're in a much worse position than we were just a couple years ago in terms of vaccination in general in the United States, and specifically with measles, which we've clearly lost control of."
